#The Digital Logos Workstation

#Part One — The instrument

#1. Hearing it together

Human knowledge has never been more abundant, or more estranged from itself. The fields that know the most barely speak to one another. A physicist and a contemplative can spend their lives on the same question — what it is to be aware of anything at all — and never read a line of each other's work. The traditions that carried wisdom for thousands of years are shelved under religion, the sciences sit in their departments, and a person's own experience is filed under nothing at all. AI could help. Mostly it is being used to make more text, faster than anyone can read it.

Lay the fields side by side, though, and they are often saying the same thing in different keys. Kepler heard the planets as harmony and computed their orbits in the same breath. When this project worked through the structure of meaning carefully enough, it found the basic intervals of music already inside it. Knowledge has a musical shape: separate voices that can be heard together without being merged into one. What has been missing is an instrument for hearing them that way, and for playing them.

Music got its instrument. Making a record once took a studio, an engineer and someone willing to pay for the hours; Ableton Live put recording, arranging, mixing and performing into one window with one clock, and now someone with a laptop can make a record in their bedroom and have strangers dancing to it by the weekend. Live did not make music easy. It made the whole craft reachable, with controls you learn once and then play with everything you have.

The Digital Logos Workstation is that instrument for knowledge, and it is built on Live's own grammar. You can read a source and keep its thread to the last citation. You can set agents to build something and watch them work. You can give an idea a form you can see and hear, and build what you find into a world someone else can walk into. And because the person doing all this is also a world — with depths that never quite rise into words — the instrument holds both: the whole that can be understood, and the self who understands it.

It isn't easy. Working this way takes reading, patience and a willingness to be corrected by your sources. But when the voices start to sound together, there is nothing like it.

#2. Worlds

Everything in the DLW is a world, and every world is drawn as a body in space.

Turn to the World and you see your own, My World, from close orbit: a planet turning slowly under its star, with the agents at work for you in orbit around it, and what they have just made drifting out on a wider ring until it is no longer new. Come down to the surface and the places on it are the things you are making. A project is a place on the ground, with paths worn between its landmarks; a book you are writing is another; a practice you keep to yourself is a room fogged to everyone but you. The day's work leaves tracks across the surface. Nothing else circles: your files, your open pages and the works you have to hand are on the ground, not in the sky.

Choose its seas and continents, how rugged the coasts run, how warm and wet the climate is, how much air and weather it has, and reroll the seed if you want a new body from the same settings. The land you build is a whole planet, with ranges, rivers, lakes, deserts, forests and ice, and it keeps its detail as you come down to it. A world you have barely begun is a grey moon; a world you have lived in for a year has seas, air and weather. Then place things on it and name them: a place, a palace you can walk into, a road between two of them, a portal through to someone else's world. Most of the building happens without your noticing. Every project you start becomes a place, and every walk you take wears a path.

The same holds in every kind of work. In Factory a task is a small world being made, its agents circling it and the helpers they spin up riding smaller orbits inside theirs, so that a whole programme of work hangs in front of you as a system you can take in at a glance. A song you are making in Live is a world, its parts the bodies in it. You can go from your day to the work you commissioned to the song you are making and never learn a new way to look.

Earth is there too, the one world nobody built. It carries real geography, and anything in your own world can be anchored to it: a letter to the town it was posted from, an idea to the house where someone first had it, a walk to the coastline it followed. You cannot reshape Earth. You place things on it, as people always have.

A collaborator's planet turns nearby. A research group is a system of planets around a shared star, and a whole discipline is a field you can pull back far enough to see entire, with the relations between worlds drawn across the dark — one anchored to another, one taking part in another, one watching, a contribution crossing the gap like a particle, two fields joined at a remove. How far you look widens a step at a time: your world alone, your world with the projects and agents it holds, the shared field, the fields that field is joined to. Whatever lies just past the edge of your view is counted and offered.

What do others see? Only what you show them. You can look at your own world as yourself, as the field sees it, or as the public sees it, and whatever you have not shown lies under cloud; raising anything into wider view asks you first. Visit someone else's world and you land on what they have shown, tinted and clouded as they left it, with the agent that keeps it there to talk to. Being findable is not being reachable. Being reachable is not being in touch, and being in touch is not being trusted — each step is separate, and each is the owner's to give. If the other world's agent gives you something, it arrives in your world under their name, and stays theirs until you have made it your own.

The field reads only what you have shown, and never owns it. If its service is lost, your own world and its open work stay exactly as they are, and when it comes back the field is brought up to date from what you had shown. Withdrawing something takes it out of the field without taking it out of your world.

So one person's work and everyone's knowledge turn out to be the same kind of thing. A private journal, a team's codebase, an archive of letters, a school of thought, the literature of a whole science: each is a world at its own distance, and you move between them by looking further out or closer in. The personal and the academic are near and far in one sky. You build your world by working in it, and as it grows it becomes something others can see, walk through and learn from. Anyone comes in the way you did: with their own work, brought in through Setup, and with their date of birth, which Nara takes as the first layer of who they are (§10.11).

Over every world there is a sky, and the sky belongs to the world. Its planets move as the real ones do; stand in today's, or in the sky of any day you choose. Two people under the same sky receive the same movements and answer them differently, because each of them is a sky as well, a whole system turning inside a person.

We are all, in a sense, aliens to one another.

#3. One grammar

If you have used Live, you already know how to hold the DLW. If you haven't, the grammar is small enough to learn in an afternoon, and once learned it does not change from one kind of work to the next. Only what it holds changes.

The grammar is Live's, used as Live uses it. A track plays. A clip is a piece of material on a track. A device dropped on a chain works on what passes through it. An instrument dropped on an empty track starts a track with it. Where something you need is not one of Live's acts, such as bringing in your work for the first time, it has a plain home of its own: a menu act, a setting, a step of setup. It never borrows a Live gesture that means something else.

Every part of the DLW that takes one of Live's meanings keeps what makes it that thing in Live. A track is a lane of one stream, with its own chain. A clip is a piece of that stream, with a state you can read. An instrument makes the material, an effect changes what passes through it and keeps the rest, a rack holds chains side by side, and a macro turns real settings of its own device. A part that cannot keep what Live's thing keeps does not take its name. Where Live has the thing, the DLW's version is checked against how Live's own behaves, as measured in Live itself.

Start with a track. In Live a track is a lane for one kind of sound — drums, a bassline, a voice — and it plays one clip at a time. In the DLW a track is a lane for one stream of your work. In Central the day is the set and each world you work in is a track — your own, a project's, a book's — and every world sends its work to the Day, the way every Live track sends its sound to the Main track. In Factory each agent session is a track. In Expressions each Expression is one. In Technē a track might be the thread of a single reading of history, or every place a subject turned up, in order.

On the track sit clips, the pieces you actually handle. A Live clip is a melody, a drum pattern, a whole song. A DLW clip is an entry in your day, a task an agent is working on, a scene in an Expression, an event at its year and place. Every clip shows its state — waiting, running, stopped, recording, stalled — so you can read a whole grid at a glance and know where things stand.

Live calls a row across the tracks a scene, and launching it starts one clip on every track at once. The DLW keeps the row and calls it a stop, because here scene always means an Expression's scene. A stop stands several things together. In Factory, firing a row launches a batch of tasks across sessions. In Technē, a stop on a walk stands a place, a moment, and the scenes that belong there. In Central, the day's face stands the entries you made while it was turned up. A stop is how you set several things going as one move.

Clips and stops live in two views of the same material. Session view is the grid: tracks across, rows down, everything launchable, nothing in any fixed order. It is where you try things, fire them, put this beside that and see what happens — a batch of tasks, a run of scenes, three passages and an answer. Arrangement view lays the same material along one ruler, so you can see the course of it: today from first entry to last, every thread of agent work with a needle showing where it has got to, an Expression's scenes in order with their sound beneath them, history from deep time to this morning. Tab moves you between the two. A third view, Pane view, holds the instruments you work in at full size: the world you stand on, a page, the torus.

Select a clip, and the bottom of the window shows it in detail. Live splits that area in two, and so does the DLW. Clip view shows the thing itself, with everything you can do to it. Device view shows what is working on it.

Clip view is where the hands get busy. In Live it holds a clip's name and colour, when and how it launches, what follows it, where it starts and ends and loops, and an editor for its notes or its sound. Each of those has a counterpart. Open a scene in Expressions and you get a roll where symbols run in lanes like notes, each step's hold and change set like a note's length and glide, with the scene's sound shown beneath it. Open a task in Factory and you get its log, every tool the agent used laid out along the task's time like notes on a bar, with what happens after it finishes and when your Stop will land. Open an event in Technē and you see its span, what it gathered, and how sure anyone is of it. Open an entry in Central and you are simply in the document, writing.

Device view shows the chain: the things working on the material, left to right, in the order the material passes through them. In Central that means the packet, the agent that answers you, what it may touch, and the world's own account of itself, its docs. In Factory it is the agent, its skills and the part of the world it may touch. The way in and the place the work lands belong to the workcell the agent works in, set once and shared by every track that works there, in every mode. In Expressions it is the studio that shapes the field. Wherever you are, the instrument in the focused pane brings its own controls into the chain.

A few of Live's quieter habits come through intact, and you will lean on them. A follow action decides what comes after a clip — the next task, the next stop, the next scene — so that things run on without you pressing each one. Launch quantize decides when a launch lands: right away, at the next bar, or, in Factory, once the agent finishes the tool it is using. Takes stack under a clip so you can choose the one that stands: the best capture of a scene, the attempt at a task that should land, the reading of a history you want to keep. Above all of it runs the transport, the same controls in the same places in every mode, each meaning what it should for the work in front of you. The views, the chain and the browser hold still in the same way: each stands where it stands in every mode, and only what it means moves with the mode.

Everything you see belongs to an owner, the product that keeps it: Central keeps your pages and your day, the engine keeps the sound, Quaternal Logic keeps the sky. The window shows what the owner reports. A change you make goes to the owner, which applies it or refuses it and says why; until it answers, the change shows as waiting. A control with no owner behind it only reads. Nothing on the screen moves without a cause you can see: whatever moves a value names itself on it.

Whatever you work on, one thing stands in focus: a constellation of your wiki, a whole and the things gathered round it, each with its source. Constellations are what last. A constellation needs no file of its own: the pages, tasks, scenes, readings and sounds made of it are what it is expressed through, and it links to each of them. No one needs to know Quaternal Logic to use one; the logic is built into the instrument, and carrying a constellation from one mode to another only transcribes it. Each mode offers the constellation in focus what that mode does. Central writes about it. Factory brings it into agentic work. Expressions gives it an expressive symbolic form. Technē lenses and refines it. Live sounds it.

The DLW has five kinds of work, its modes, and the transport switches between them. Live is the base, where the instrument is played. Central is where the day's work gathers. Factory is where agents build. Expressions is where a thing takes a form you can see and hear. Technē is where knowledge is built into worlds. Epi-Logos is not a sixth mode: it lies over all five, and Nara's practice belongs to it (§13).

The modes are one environment, not five tools that share files. What you make in one becomes material in another and keeps where it came from. A passage you read in Central becomes the source of a task you commission in Factory. A sweep of the field in Expressions becomes a stop on a walk in Technē. A palace you build in Technē returns to Central's wiki as a proposal. Changing mode keeps what you selected and closes nothing, and a crossing never sends, shows or launches anything by itself. Each clip's source is its constellation, as a sample is a Live audio clip's: select a clip in any mode and its Clip panel names the constellation, and Show in Browser keeps it in front of you as you change mode (§10.3).

#4. Three times

Whatever you are working with, you can meet it in three times.

Live is the thing as it happens: agents moving around the task they are building, the field breathing on its pulse, your planet changing under your hands. It is Session view's time — things launched and running, you listening and answering.

Take it into your hands and it is composed. You order the stops of a walk, build a scene until the figure says what you meant, drag a graph into the shape of an argument. That is Clip view's work, and you can do it in the present or step back into a past moment, a chosen day's sky, and compose there.

What you keep is recorded — a take, a walk laid along the ruler, a day closed into what it taught. It sits in Arrangement view to be edited, played back, and given to someone who will play it in their own world, where it is live again.

#5. Central — the day's work

You need one place where the day's work gathers by itself, where the parts of your life you are working on are to hand, and where you write what only you can add.

Central is where the day happens. It looks and works like a code editor, after VS Code's workbench — your worlds and their pages down the left, documents open side by side, a terminal a click away — except that the day itself is one of the documents, and it fills itself in. Everything you do across the DLW leaves its mark there as you go: the passages you read and marked, the tasks you set going in Factory and what came back from them, the scene you composed, the walk you recorded, the conversation you had in someone else's world. By evening the day has gathered the whole of it into one structured page, and you add what only you can — what you noticed, what didn't work and why, what you want to remember. The work and your account of the work end up in the same place, and the evening never has to reconstruct the morning.

Today is a set, as a song is in Live, and every world you touch today has a track in it. Say you are writing a book. Its world is a track, and the people in it, the objects and sources it turns on and the conversations you have about it are that track's clips. Open the chapter's flow and it plays, with the agent you were talking to back in its seat; open a person and you can read them, walk to where they lived, or find them in the sky. Whatever is still playing is what is open now. It carries into tomorrow's set until you close it, while everything you opened and wrote lays itself down along the day's timeline, so that by evening the Day's arrangement is the day as you lived it. The Day itself sits at the end of the grid, where Live keeps its Main track, and every world sends its work there.

How you read is kept apart from what you read. Under the browser, where Live keeps its grooves, the pool holds QL frames and MEF lenses: ways of reading a page that change nothing in it, and that serve any clip in any mode. The window you work in is kept with the day's set, and comes back as you left it.

Every document in Central starts from a template, and every template is yours to change. A Day is shaped like a die, four faces for the work and two at its edges, and you turn it face by face as the day moves. A Flow is a running conversation or journal, with the people and agents in it named at the top. Beings and Things are the people and objects your work is about, each tied to the world it belongs to, its sources, and the real place where it stands. Restyle them, add sections, build new kinds of your own. However a page looks, it keeps its connections: a Day you have redesigned still fills itself, and a Thing you have rearranged still knows where it stands on the map.

Type @ and you are speaking Central's own search language. At its simplest it finds anything you can reach — a person, an agent, a place, a document, a passage — and sends what you have selected there. Highlight a paragraph and tag a colleague, and it reaches them as a message carrying the passage and where it came from. Tag an agent and it starts working on it. Tag a place and the passage is filed on that spot of your world. Past the simple uses it is a language with a grammar you grow into, and you make your own aliases in it, so that a short name you chose stands for a long search you use every day. Like anything worth learning on an instrument, it rewards the hours you give it.

Select a passage and the rest is close at hand: highlight it, note it, put it in the packet, or ask about it now. The packet is exactly what the agent will read; you see it whole, and how big it is, before anything is sent. Press Play and the agent answers into the page as a new entry with its sources, and any source followed back lands you on the line it came from. Press Record and talk, and your words go into the document. Overdub decides whether what comes back joins as a new entry or replaces the one you selected.

The agent never writes behind your back. With Arm off, anything it wants to change arrives as a proposal; arm it, and its edits land directly, each with a receipt. Change a passage the agent wrote and a light comes on, so that one press can hand it back. Tap stamps the moment into whatever you have open.

Turn to the world instrument and Central is your planet. Projects are places on its surface. The day's work is a walk across it, marked wherever something mattered, and whatever you are holding — open files, the context gathered for an agent — circles overhead and drops away when you are finished with it. On the world's graph side you see what today touched; in the knowledge graph you can follow your notes link by link into everything you have already written.

Then the day closes itself. What you learned is filed into your knowledge, what you made is kept, and tomorrow begins on a clean face of the die. No hours are set: Central keeps the day's bounds.

In Central you:

  • write about the constellation in focus;
  • bring the worlds you work on into today, and pick each up where you left it;
  • read and write their pages, and mark what matters in them;
  • hand a passage to an agent, and keep or refuse what it proposes;
  • find anything you can reach with @, and send what you selected there;
  • keep each world's own account of itself, from its origin to its evidence;
  • see the day written down as you lived it, and add what only you know;
  • let the day close into what it taught.

#6. Factory — worlds making worlds

You need to set agents to work on something larger than one session can hold, see how every part of it stands, and step in only where you are needed.

Factory is where you work with AI agents, through an agent client built after Grok Bot's. Say what you want built — software, a body of research, a place for others to stand in — and the work breaks into tasks that agents take up while you watch the floor, stepping in where you are needed and staying out of the way where you aren't.

Each agent works a track, and its tasks are the clips. Drag an agent from the browser onto an empty track and it takes the seat. Fire a task and it runs; fire a row and a batch starts across every session at once. How a task is drawn tells you how it stands. A running task has no end, because nobody knows yet how long it will take, and a queued one has no length at all. A stalled task is striped and frozen where its output stopped, and its track lights a retry. Groups of agents fold under one header, and each agent's helpers step in beneath it, a coloured rail for every level, so three layers of delegation read at a glance.

In Arrangement view the work moves. Every thread runs along one ruler with a needle that jumps each time its agent checks in, and a needle that stops moving is a stall. Under each thread run its messages, the files it touched, its terminal, the pages it read; click any of them and it opens beside you.

Select a session and its chain shows what works on it, left to right. First the agent itself: its model, how much it decides alone, how hard it thinks, how many turns it gets. Then its skills, racked with a light each: you ask for a skill on or off, the rack shows whether it is loaded and what it has done, and a preview shows the change before you apply it. Then the part of the world it may touch, from one object up to everything you own, and whether what it writes there arrives as a proposal, a draft or a change. Swap any device, add a skill, drop a whole team of agents onto the chain as a rack of its own.

The road in and out belongs to the workcell the session works in, which stands where Live keeps its return tracks. In through a gateway, which decides how the agent reaches the program that runs it and what it must ask your permission for; onto the machine that carries it; into its seat in the project; and out through the landing: commits, and a request to merge with the checks that tested it. Set it once, and every session that works there takes it, in every mode.

The transport becomes the foreman's desk. Play runs the work. Stop pauses at the next safe point and keeps what every agent had in mind; press it twice to cancel. With Steer on, what you type reaches an agent mid-turn, and with it off your words wait as the next task. Arm decides whether agents write directly or propose. Draw a window across a task and nothing is written before you approve the plan or after it ships. Capture records what you do by hand so an agent can learn it from you, and Tap asks every running agent where it has got to, the answers coming back to the rail, where your agents stand at their stations like a hive.

Seen as a world, a piece of work is a planet in the making. The task is the world, its agents move in orbit around it, and their helpers ride smaller orbits inside theirs; a whole programme is a system of such worlds, some settled, some still forming. Lay that programme out as a graph and it becomes a map of what waits on what — how you plan the next stretch, and how you find where it is stuck.

When a world is finished, it doesn't hang there. Some finished work becomes a workflow, the same steps ready to run again on new material. Some becomes a loop that studies its own results and runs better next time. And some worlds simply complete: what they made passes on into the places that needed it, and the world itself folds away.

In Factory you:

  • bring the constellation in focus into agentic work;
  • say what you want built, and see it broken into tasks;
  • seat agents on tracks, and fire their tasks one at a time or a row at once;
  • see at a glance which task waits, runs, stalls or is done, and retry a stall;
  • tune each agent: its model, its effort, its skills and what it may touch;
  • decide once where agents work, on which machine, and how their work lands;
  • steer, pause or stop the work, and approve what agents propose;
  • keep finished work as a workflow to run again.

#7. Expressions — the living medium

You need to give a thing a form you can see and hear, and to stay with it until it says what you meant.

Expressions edits as a video editor does, and its medium is a living field. You cut scenes on a timeline, and what the scenes are made of is the particle field, glyphs, and the text you lay over them. Audio and video tracks share the one timeline, so a scene's picture and its sound are cut together.

Expressions is a medium you step into rather than look at. Text, symbols, image, physics and sound share one field. Particles gather into the shapes you give them and move by the forces you set; symbols hold their places or drift, pull on one another or push apart. Beneath the field lies a plate — in three dimensions, a chamber — and as you sweep it you hear the pattern forming on its surface. The pitch rides the lines where the plate stands still, and each symbol can carry a small voice tuned to its own frequency. Sound and image rise from the same moving state, so when one changes, the other changes with it.

You build in scenes. An Expression holds its scenes the way a Live track holds its clips: launch them, loop them, layer one over another, record them. Open a scene and you have both its sides in front of you — the sequence step by step, each symbol in its own lane like a note on a roll, each step's hold and change set like a note's length and glide, and beneath it what the scene sounds like. Add a voice, pin its force, turn the plate on and sweep it until the figure says what you meant. Take the swell, layer the next section over it, capture the figure as a new scene, and save.

What belongs to one scene is in the scene itself, open below the field: its length and what it carries, what follows it, the tools that draw a form, bind a symbol, arrange several or tie six into one figure, and the symbol you have selected, with its place, its force, its voice and its meaning. What shapes the field is in the device area. The studio holds the controls you chose to play, the same in every scene, and the devices that govern the field itself — physics, the pointer, how symbols relate, the medium they move through, what happens when they touch, morph, focus, colour, ink, depth, resonance — in four chains: material, motion, body, and a personal layer that stays yours however the scene is shared. Each is a whole device with every setting it needs. Read one at a glance on its chain, open it as a band above the chain with every setting, let it fill a pane or a window of its own, or keep it as a tile on the rail. Open the studio's own pane beside the field and every device stands in it at once, with the controls you chose at its head. Its settings stay live whichever you look at.

The transport turns in this case to the field. Tempo is the speed it forms and breathes at, and the time signature is the scene's ratio of hold to change. Key is the resonance the field is tuned to, which can be taken from the sky over your world so that colours and intervals shift as the planets move. Play plays the scenes. Arm the studio and Play records a take; record several, and keep the one that stands.

Agents can express through this medium as well. An interface built for them lets an agent open an Expression, compose in it and perform it, so that what an agent finds can reach you as something you see and hear. The library of Expressions people make is how agents learn it: it shows them what an expression is, and how differently two people can give form to the same thing.

An agent can teach this way too. Ask Epii to explain a relation you have selected and it composes a short sequence in the field, not a long answer beside it: it sets out the things that carry the relation, moves between them with a few words, and says how it is reading them. Pause it, open a source, ask a question, or turn the reading down and go on; what you turn down is kept as turned down. Whatever an agent changes in the field is tied to the act that changed it, so movement you see is never taken for work an agent did, and an agent asked to change one thing leaves your scenes, your locks and your own edits as they were.

Anything in any mode can be given an expression — a day, a run of work, a source, a place, an argument you can't yet put into words — and every mode can open the expression stage beside its own panes. Scenes made here travel: onto a walk, into a palace, into someone else's world. Live joins this medium on one timeline, sound and picture together, the way a film editor holds them.

An Expression can live inside a page. A being, a thing, a flow or a day can hold one playing; open it full and it is the same Expression, and closing it brings you back to the page where you were. Where it cannot play live, the page shows its still or its recording and says so. Open a coordinate of the map as an Expression and the whole field is expressed from that place, with its sources a step away; an Expression made this way from the readings says that it was generated, while one you compose keeps the sources it was made from. Close the DLW and open it again, and an Expression's scenes, settings and selection come back as you saved them; the field tells you what of its live motion it could not bring back.

And you can simply stay with it. Turn the lights down, let a single symbol turn in the field and listen to what it does.

In Expressions you:

  • give the constellation in focus an expressive symbolic form;
  • compose a scene: its symbols in lanes, each step's hold and change, its sound;
  • cut scenes on one timeline, with audio and video tracks together;
  • shape the field: what it is made of, how it moves, its body, and your own layer over it;
  • play scenes, layer them, and keep the take that stands;
  • give anything from any mode an expression, and carry scenes onto walks, into palaces and into other worlds;
  • let an agent show what it found as something you see and hear;
  • stay with the field and listen.

#8. Technē — crafting knowledge

You need to make knowledge that you and others can walk into: a subject set at its places and in its times, with every source kept, and readings that disagree laid side by side.

Technē is where knowledge is made by building worlds. Find a subject and gather what surrounds it: the people involved, the places, the sources and what they claim. Set it on the Earth where it happened and under the sky it happened beneath, lay its history along the ruler, walk its places in order, and build it a palace someone else can enter. Places, peoples and agents, ways of seeing, the journeys between them: here they are the material itself.

Why build knowledge like this? Because that is how people have always held it. We remember by place — the old art of memory set each thing to be remembered in a room of an imagined building, and a walk through the rooms brought it all back. We understand by time, by seeing what came before and what followed and what happened at once. And we think by relation, by putting one thing next to another and seeing that they belong together. A page of text holds these things flat. Technē gives each its own dimension, so that you can see where an idea lived, when it changed, what it touched, and walk through it in an order that makes sense. Everything you place carries its source and its owner, so a reader can always go back and check. And because each reading of a subject is a layer laid over the others, never a replacement for them, people who disagree can work on the same ground, with the disagreement in plain view. That is a different culture of knowledge from the one we have: shared without being flattened, open to anyone willing to walk it.

Everything starts from the world. Pull back and you see the field of worlds turning around their stars. Come in, and a single body fills the pane, then a region, then one place with its exact position and the frame it was measured in. Turn the world to its graph side and the same material lays out by connection, each thing coloured by what it is, the ties between them showing what joins them. Build your own planet here — its seas and continents, climate and sky, and the places, palaces, roads and portals you set on it. Earth is given; you place things on it, and anchor your own world's places to its real ones.

The canvas is where you think out loud. Throw ideas onto it, drag them into clusters, draw a frame around a group, run a line from one thing to another to say they belong together, and keep going until the shape of the problem shows. It works the way a mind map does, with a difference: everything on it is a real thing you can open, and a line you draw stays a suggestion until whoever owns that relation agrees to it.

Arrangement view is Technē's timeline. It sets history beside the work that studied it, on one ruler that measures either the time of your sessions or the history of what you study, from deep time to this morning. One person's reading of an age is a layer of tracks, and a later reading lies over it without erasing it. Ages nest inside ages, and the narrowest colours everything inside it. Read the same events by date, by cause, by what keeps recurring, or by what happened at once. Everything keeps the weight it has — fact, claim, inference, guess, dispute, or a gap nobody has filled — and setting two things side by side never turns a coincidence into a cause.

The journey is an ordered walk through places, moments and things, with a pace, a way of arriving at each stop, and a voice that tells it. The palace gives a whole subject a building to live in: rooms that each hold a part of it, a path through them, a guide who explains why each room is there, a private room that stays clouded, and doors out to other places and other people's worlds.

A walk is where all of these meet. Take a thread from the timeline and walk it, and each stop sets the clock to its year and the world to its place, and launches the scenes it carries — an image, a film, a living field. A walk can pass through several Expressions, one scene from each, or step down through the scenes of one. Press Record and go somewhere new; your stops become the walk's stops, and it lays itself along the ruler, ready to edit and ready to give away.

A lens is one way of seeing. Quaternal Logic has twelve, and the Lens reads a subject through one of them at a time. It shows where that way of seeing reaches and where it stops, and it never changes what it reads.

Above the world the sky turns. Stand in today's, or in the sky of any date you choose, and work there; one tap brings you back to now. The transport walks: tempo is the walk's pace, the time signature tells you which stop of how many, quantize decides how each stop arrives. Key is how far you are looking and as whom — your own world, the shared field or beyond; as yourself, as the field, as the public. Beside the instruments works a companion, Epi, who stays with you on the rail in every mode (§10.6): it reads the sources with you, proposes what might follow, and can tell you why any room in a palace stands where it does.

In Technē you:

  • lens and refine the constellation in focus;
  • gather a subject: its people, places, sources and claims, each with its owner;
  • set it on Earth and under the sky it happened beneath;
  • lay its history along the ruler, and read it by date, by cause, by what recurs or by what happened at once;
  • think it out on the canvas;
  • walk it in order, and record the walk to give away;
  • build it a palace someone else can enter;
  • read it through one lens at a time.

#9. Live — the instrument

You need an instrument you can play: the sound of the logic itself, from a keyboard, with every part of it yours to shape and keep.

At the heart of the DLW is one instrument, and Live mode is where you play it.

It is a torus, turning in the centre of the pane, and what you see is the sound itself: a field of vibration wound around a ring, its surface patterned by what it is doing. Two pulses drive it, beating against each other, and everything you hear comes from them. Touch the surface and it rings. Play a note and a point on the ring lights and answers; play a chord and several points light together, and the figure they draw on the surface is the chord's shape — the same shape the DLW uses for the symbol that chord belongs to. Play a symbol and you hear its harmony. Play its harmony and the symbol appears.

You play it from a keyboard laid out in six rows, two families of whole tones interleaved so that every semitone is a short step across and every chord has the same fingering in every key. Wrap those two rows around the ring and they become the torus's two helices, which is why a key on the keyboard and a point on the torus are the same thing. Use a mouse, your fingers, the computer keyboard or a MIDI controller; or switch to an ordinary piano layout if you would rather.

Choose the mode you are playing in and the keyboard and the piano roll follow it, marking the notes that belong and folding away the ones that don't. The modes reach from the plain diatonic scale to the full set the logic generates, and beside them sit older scales that keep their own intervals and their own history: the planetary scales Marsilio Ficino composed in, meant to draw each planet's quality into whoever heard them; the Shem scales; the maqām. Over the instrument turns the sky of your world, and each planet can move a part of the sound — its own interval, its own colour — shown on the control it is moving.

The mode lives where Live keeps its scales. Set it in the transport and the whole set plays in it: root, mode and tuning, with the keyboard recoloured to match. Open a clip and it can carry a mode of its own, so a piece can move from one to another phrase by phrase, and the roll folds to that clip's notes or highlights them in place. In the chain, devices work on the notes before they reach the torus — one bends whatever you play onto the mode, one sets the tuning in exact ratios, one hands parts of the sound to the planets overhead — and you can stack, reorder and save them like any other.

Shape the sound as far as you like. Every part of the instrument is a setting you can turn, record and save, and a saved state is a sound you can return to, share or start from. Put devices on its chain to filter it, echo it, give it a room to sound in, or ring it through the Resonator bank, which sounds the M3 clock's cut of the octave after the torus (§22.7). Record what you play, edit it note by note in the roll, layer it, loop it, arrange it into a piece.

The same torus turns at the centre of every Expression, so what you play here can be heard and seen there, inside a scene, and the two share one timeline, picture and sound together.

In Live you:

  • sound the constellation in focus;
  • play the torus from its keyboard, a controller, or its surface;
  • choose the mode you play in, for the whole set or for one clip;
  • let the sky over your world move parts of the sound;
  • shape the sound with devices, and keep it as a state to return to;
  • ring the M3 clock's cut through the Resonator bank;
  • record, edit, layer and arrange what you play.

#10. Working the window

Everything in this section is the same in every kind of work. Learn it once.

Ease of use comes first, in every mode. What you do most is one act, in the place you would look for it. Each function has one home, and each device is named for what you do with it. A device's folded face answers one plain need; its depth waits in its pages and its Full view, for when you go looking.

#10.1 The window

The window has six parts, and each has one job. The transport across the top runs things. The browser down the left holds what you can bring in. The main area in the middle holds the work of the mode you are in. The widget rail on the right keeps what you want at hand. The detail area along the bottom shows what is selected and the chain that works on it. The status bar at the foot says what a control does.

Part What it is for
Transport Start, stop, record and set the pace of whatever you are working on. Choose the kind of work and the view.
Browser Find material, instruments, devices and running things, and bring them in (§10.3).
Main area Hold the mode's work in one of three views: Session view, Arrangement view or Pane view (§10.2).
Widget rail Keep context at hand in every kind of work: the agent you are talking to, the packet, the trail, a terminal, the sky.
Detail area See the selected clip in Clip view, and the chain that works on it in Device view, one above the other.
Status bar Read what a control does, or what went wrong, in one line. Switch Clip view, Device view and the mixer.

#The transport

Every control has one place in the transport, and the place is the same in every mode. A control that a mode does not use stays in its place, dimmed, so that nothing slides into its space. From the left:

Group Controls
Browser Show or hide the browser.
Time Link, Tap, Tempo, Time signature, Metronome, Quantize.
Key Key, root and scale.
Position Follow, then Position.
Play Play, Stop, Record.
Recording Overdub, Arm, Re-enable, Capture.
Loop Where the loop starts, Punch in, Loop, Punch out, and the loop's length.
Hands Draw, the playing keys, Key map, MIDI map.
Readings Rate, Load.
Mode Live, Central, Factory, Expressions, Technē.
View Session, Arrangement, Pane.
Rail Show or hide the widget rail.

What each control does in each mode is in §10.5. Above the controls, the title line names what you have selected, its world and its day, with Back and Forward at its head (§10.7). The moment you stand in shows in Position. Instruments are not in the transport: they come from the browser. Settings open in a window of their own with ⌘, as Live's do, and never take the main area (§10.10).

#The bottom right

You switch Clip view and Device view where Live does, at the right end of the status bar.

Control What it does
Clip Brings Clip view forward. The switch carries a small picture of the selected clip. ▲ beside it shows or hides Clip view.
Device Brings Device view forward. The switch carries the selected track's name and a small picture of its chain. ▲ beside it shows or hides Device view. Right-click it for a list of the chain's devices, and choose one to go to it.
Mixer Shows or hides the mixer row of every track (§16.6).

⌥-click Clip or Device to show both views at once, one above the other. When only one shows, ⇧Tab switches to the other. The rest of the status bar is one line: what the control under the pointer does, or what went wrong.

#Showing, hiding and sizing

The browser, the rail and the detail area work alike. Each has a toggle at the edge it stands on, a key, and an edge you drag to size it. Hide one and the main area takes its room. Show it again and it comes back at the size you left it.

A part you have hidden is a way of holding the window, not something missing. Nothing reports it as missing and nothing opens it for you; show it again and it comes back as you left it, with what changed meanwhile read again in place.

Part Toggle Key To size it
Browser Top left ⌥⌘B or ⌥⌘5 Drag its right edge.
Pool The foot of the browser ⌥⌘6 Drag the line between it and the browser.
Widget rail Top right ⌥⌘8 Drag its left edge.
Clip view ▲ beside Clip, bottom right ⌥⌘3 Drag the line above the detail area.
Device view ▲ beside Device, bottom right ⌥⌘4 Drag the line above the detail area.
Clip view and Device view together — ⌥⌘L —
Mixer Mixer, bottom right ⌥⌘M —

⌃⌘F lets the window fill the screen.

#Where a session lives

A terminal and an agent's session each live in a session space: one lasting place of work, kept by AIKit, which the window shows but does not own. A space is a room, not a self. The agent working in it is the same agent wherever the room is shown. A space outlives the window: close the window and the work goes on in its room; open it again and you come back to the same room.

herdr, tmux, cmux and your computer's own terminal are providers of a space. Each can show it, and the names each gives it are labels, never who it is. If one provider stops answering, only its view of the space goes dark.

A room lives as long as the machine that holds it. If a provider restarts, or the machine under it, the space tells you what came back: the room's layout, the history on its screen, the agent's own session taken up again, or a fresh agent given the same work. Whichever it is, the work keeps its identity, and a room rebuilt after a restart is never shown as the old one still running. A name or a number that turns up again does not make it the same room.

Opening a room that runs on another of your machines leaves the work where it runs (§19.18). Moving it is a different act: you change the workcell its track works in, and the next task starts there (§19.23).

A Terminal follows the room of the workcell its track works in. A message to an agent goes to the agent through Messages (§10.6). It never types into the agent's room.

#10.2 Session view, Arrangement view and Pane view

Each mode has one set of tracks, and the main area shows it in one of three views. Session view lays the tracks across a grid of clips that you launch in any order. Arrangement view lays the same tracks along one ruler, so that you can follow the course of the work. Pane view holds the instruments you work in at full size: the world you stand on, a page, a graph, the torus.

Switch with Session, Arrangement and Pane at the right of the transport, or with the keys:

To Press
Switch between Session view and Arrangement view Tab. From Pane view, Tab returns to the view you left.
Show Pane view ⌥⌘9. Press it again to return to the view you left.
Open a second window ⇧⌘W. Each window shows its own view of the same set, as Live's second window does: the grid on one screen, the ruler or the panes on the other.

A mode has one selection: a track, a clip, a row, a stretch of time or a device. Every view and the detail area show the same one, and switching changes only what you see. What you selected stays selected, and what runs keeps running: a task launched in Session view runs on while you read its course in Arrangement view. Clip view keeps the selected clip. Where the clip has a place in the view you switch to, that place is selected and scrolled into sight. Where it has none, as with a task that has not yet run, its track's head lights. The browser, the rail and the detail area stay as they were.

Only Clip view can take the main area from these three. Press ⌥⌘E and Clip view fills the main area while you edit. Press it again and the view you left comes back as it was.

#Pane view

Panes let you keep several things in front of you at once: a document beside the day it belongs to, an agent's thread beside the files it is changing, a walk beside the palace it passes through.

A pane holds one device's Full view: its material at full size, with no controls on it (§16.3). The controls stay in Device view below. Focus a pane, and Device view shows the chain the device stands on, with the device selected. A device that stands on no chain shows there alone.

To open an instrument, drag it from the browser into a pane. You can also click it, and it opens in the pane that has focus. To split a pane, click ⊞. Then select Beside, Below or Four ways. To move a tab, drag it onto the centre of another pane. To make a new split, drag a tab onto the edge of a pane. Double-click a pane's tab and the pane fills the main area; double-click it again and the other panes come back.

A pane follows what you select, unless you pin it. A pinned pane keeps its subject while you work elsewhere.

Some instruments come in more than one build, the way Live has more than one reverb. Each build answers to the same controls, so you can change the build without losing your settings.

A layout is how a mode's window stands: the view in front, the panes and what they hold, the widgets on the rail, and the sizes of the browser, the rail and the detail area. Each set keeps its own layout: open the set, and the window stands as you left it. An arrangement you want to start from again is a template in the browser (§10.3).

#The three views side by side

Session view Arrangement view Pane view
For Trying things: launching clips in any order, setting several going at once, keeping today's work to hand. Following and shaping the course of the work: what happened, in what order, and for how long. Working in the material itself, at full size.
What it acts on Tracks, clips, empty slots, rows and the Main track. Tracks, clips in time and the lanes under them, markers, the loop brace, and stretches of time. The device in each pane, and the material inside it: a page's words, a world's places, a graph's nodes.
What you do there Launch and stop clips and rows. Start a clip in an empty slot. Drag clips between slots. Group and fold tracks. Place, move, trim and split clips. Select a stretch of time. Audition takes and comp them. Draw automation. Set the loop. Open, split, move and pin panes. Work the material with the instrument's own tools.
Selecting Click a clip, a slot, a track's head or a row. The arrow keys move the selection. Click a clip or a lane, or drag across a stretch of time. Select inside the instrument. What you select there that is a clip, such as a stop of a walk in the Journey, is the mode's selected clip.
Focus ⌥1 ⌥2 ⌥9
Starting things Enter, or a clip's ▶, launches the clip. A row's ▶ launches the row. Space plays from the insert marker, and a clip plays when the playhead reaches it. Space plays the transport, and the instrument plays what the transport plays.
Its forms Tracks narrow or wide, groups folded or open, the mixer row shown or hidden. Tracks folded to one line or open with their lanes, zoomed from the whole span to one clip, with the overview strip above. One pane, two beside or below each other, or four; or one pane filling the area.
While it loads The tracks it last showed stand at once. Slots still being read are dimmed. The ruler and the tracks stand at once. Clips still being read are dimmed. Each pane shows its device's last picture, dimmed, until the device answers.
Empty The grid waits for a drop: a world in Central, an agent in Factory, an Expression in Expressions. The ruler waits for what you record or place. An empty pane waits for an instrument from the browser.
Switched off A deactivated clip is grey and does not launch. A track whose activator is off is dimmed. A deactivated clip is grey, and the playhead passes it by. A device that is off draws its material dimmed.
When its owner cannot be reached The tracks keep what was last read, dimmed, and nothing launches. The same, on the ruler. The pane keeps its device's last picture, dimmed, and the device's light is dark.
When something fails What failed stays as it was last read. One line in the status bar says what failed. The same. The same.
What is kept The set is kept by its owner: its tracks, its clips, their order and their settings. How you look at it is kept with the set: the view in front, sizes, folds, zoom, and the panes with what they hold. The same. The same.

The part with focus has a bright edge, and the keys act on what is selected in it. ⌥0 moves focus to the transport, ⌥3 to Clip view, ⌥4 to Device view, ⌥5 to the browser and ⌥6 to the pool, as in Live. A drag, an open menu, a value you are typing, and Clip view expanded into the main area last only while you use them.

Looking away unloads nothing. Come back to a pane, a set or a mode you left and it is there at once as you left it, scrolled and selected where you were. What changed while you were away is read again in place, with the last reading standing until the new one arrives, and a slow folder in the browser never holds back a page you already know.

If the DLW stops without warning, it opens again on what it kept: the set, its panes and what they held, and the writing it had kept on this machine but not yet saved, back on its page beside the revision it began from. A part of the window it cannot read is set aside with its reason while the rest opens; it is never replaced by an empty window. A page changed elsewhere in the meantime shows as a conflict, never as a quiet replacement of what you wrote.

#10.3 The browser and the pool

You need to find anything you can work with and bring it in, without learning a new list in each mode. There is one browser, after Live's, and it is the same in every mode. Only what leads it changes.

It holds four kinds of thing:

Kind What it holds To use it
Material What the work is made of: the constellations of your wiki, worlds and their pages, earlier Days, sessions and their chats, Expressions and their scenes, sources, sets and their templates, and the recordings, renders and imports the sets use. Double-click it, or drag it into a pane, to open it. Drag it onto an empty track to bring it into the set: a world joins today, a chat's session reopens where it stopped. Drag a constellation onto a track and the mode makes its own clip of it. Drag a chat onto the rail to talk in it.
Instruments What makes a track's material: the Agent, the Document, the World, the Journey, the Field, the Torus and the others, each with its presets under it, as Live keeps a device's presets. Your agents and the agent types stand under the Agent; saved sounds under the Torus. Drag it into a pane to open it. Drag it onto an empty track to start a track with it: an agent dropped there takes the seat.
Devices What works on a chain or stands on the rail: effects, racks such as skillsets and agentsets, modulators, connections such as gateways, and monitors with their widgets. Drag it onto a chain to add it there, or onto the rail to keep it at hand. A widget is installed from here.
Running things What is running now: agents at work, open sessions, workcells and the machines that hold them. Work with it where it is. Select it to follow it; drag it onto the rail to keep it at hand.

Preview, open and add are separate acts. Select a row once and its preview shows at the foot of the list, where Live plays a sample you select: a page's first lines, a material's picture, a device's account of what it does, a chat's last exchange. A preview changes nothing. Opening and adding are the drags above.

A constellation's preview is what this mode makes of it: in Central, the writing about it; in Factory, the work it would become; in Expressions, its symbolic form; in Technē, its reading through a lens; in Live, its sound. Each clip's source is its constellation, as a sample is a Live audio clip's (§16.5). Show in Browser, beside the constellation in a clip's Clip panel and in the clip's menu, selects the constellation here, as Live's Show in Browser selects a clip's sample. Change mode and it stays selected, and its preview shows what the new mode makes of it. Drag it onto a track and this mode makes its own clip of it, with the constellation as its source: a page in Central, a task in Factory, a scene in Expressions, an event in Technē, a clip in Live.

Down the browser's left side stand Live's three groups: Collections, the coloured favourites you make; the four kinds above, as Live's categories; and Places, where your ground lies.

Place What it holds
You My World, your Days, and the identity you share.
Agents The agents of your roster, accepted and proposed, with the harnesses and skills they carry.
Machines Your machines, and the workcells each one holds.
Work Your projects, each a world with its pages. Add folder… brings in another (§10.11).

Each mode's browser leads with the material its work is made of. The other kinds follow in the same order in every mode.

Mode What leads the browser
Live Your sets, and the Torus's saved sounds.
Central Your whole field: every world, each opening to its pages; Earth and the worlds you visit; the earlier Days. Central is where you work across your projects, so the list is not divided by project.
Factory Your projects, each opening to its chats: the sessions you had there, newest first, each with its agent, its state and its last exchange.
Expressions Your Expressions, each opening to its scenes; then the library and its starters.
Technē Your sources; then the bodies, places, palaces and journeys of the world you stand in.

What you brought in at setup stands where you would look for it: your ground under You, your agents with their harnesses and skills under Agents, your machines under Machines, your projects under Work. How each is set up stands in Settings (§10.10). A credential is never in the browser. Settings shows its reference, and never its value.

#Sets, files and media

A project is a folder, and its constellation is its index. A node of the constellation needs no file: the files in the folder are its expressions, each kept in the format of the mode that made it. Central keeps pages as Markdown and HTML, Expressions keeps an Expression as JSON, and Live reads and writes a real .als that Ableton Live opens. Carrying a thing from one mode to another transcribes it, and nothing is converted.

The set is a file of the DLW's own, kept in the project. Its clips refer to the constellation's nodes, never to copies of them, and it keeps the layout of the window it was worked in. Open Set… (⌘O), Save Set (⌘S) and Save Set As… (⇧⌘S) stand in the File menu, as they do in Live, and a set is named by its file. The DLW reopens the world you chose with its own sets as you left them; a set from another world, or a copy a test left behind, is never reopened as remembered state. In Central the set is today's Day, and saving it is the day's close (§18.1).

A set you want to start from again is a template. Choose Save Set as Template… in the File menu, and the template stands in the browser with your sets. A new set started from it takes its tracks and its layout.

Media come in three kinds. A recording is source material. A render is made from something else: it names what it was made from, it can be remade, and it is never edited in place. When the source of a render has moved since it was made, the render's row in the browser says so, and Remake, in its menu, makes it again from the source as it now stands. An import keeps where it came from. The set refers to its media by paths inside the project, and large media is held by its content hash, out of git.

#The pool

Under the browser is the pool, where Live keeps its Groove Pool. A groove shapes how a clip plays without being part of the clip, and the pool holds what shapes how a clip is read without being part of it: QL frames and MEF lenses, the DLW's grooves. A frame is the form of a whole and the roles round it (§17.4); a lens is one of Quaternal Logic's ways of seeing (§17.11). Drop a constellation onto the pool and its frame and its lenses stand there, the way a clip dropped on Live's pool gives up its groove. Choose one in a clip's Clip panel, where Live's Groove stands, and the clip is read through it; the clip's source does not change. In Live the pool also holds the set's grooves, as Live's does (§16.7).

The pool shows nothing else. A device opens whole in its band above the chain, and an instrument opens in a pane.

#10.4 Devices

A device does one job to the material in front of it. An instrument makes something new: an agent answers, the field moves, the torus rings. An effect changes what passes through it and keeps the rest: a highlight marks a passage and leaves the passage whole. Devices sit left to right in a chain, and the material always passes through them in that order.

A rack holds several chains side by side under one device, with a selector to choose between them. An agent's skills sit in a rack, and so do the agents of a team. A macro is one knob that turns several settings at once, each within its own range.

Three kinds of device work beside the chain rather than in its line. A modulator moves other devices' settings from a clock of its own: the planets overhead turning a filter on the torus. A monitor shows what is happening and writes nothing: the files an agent is changing, the frames it sends, your own trail through the day. A connection brings an agent to its work and takes the work to where it lands: the gateway to the program that runs the agent, the machine that carries it, the seat where it changes a project, the landing that commits and merges. The connections of one workcell are set once, and every agent that works there uses them, in every mode.

A device has up to six views, all showing the same live settings. It has the views of the places it stands in: a monitor, which stands only on the rail and in a pane, has two.

View Where What you get
Folded Your chain, along the bottom The device's name and a reading or two, in a narrow strip
Compact Your chain A small live picture and up to four controls
Whole Expanded above the chain Every setting, grouped, round a larger picture
Full A pane The device's material at full size, to work in
Pop-out Its own window, which can fill the screen The material with every setting under it
Widget The rail on the right A small picture and a few readings, in every mode

The head opens a device each way. ▸ beside its light shows its expanded view, a band above the chain, as Live's does; ▦ opens it in a pane, and ↗ pops it out into a window, as Live opens a plug-in. Double-click the head to fold the device to its title. Select a device in the browser to read what it does; drag it onto a chain to use it.

A light on a device is a reading. It is on only when the device reports that it is on. If the state is not known, the light stays dark.

When something moves a value, the value shows what moved it. An agent's edit carries the agent's name. A knob that the sky is turning shows the planet that turns it. If you take hold of something an agent or instrument was holding, the hand-back light comes on. Press it to give control back.

You can build new devices that sit in the same chain, as Max for Live devices do in Live. Each part of the suite brings its own devices: the day and its documents, the agents and what tunes them, the skills they carry, the work they do, the machines they run on, and the sky and its clock.

#Houses

You do a few things many times, so each is done in one place. Devices that serve one concern stand together as a house, and making a thing is using that thing's own device on something new: an agent is made in the Agent, a group in the Agentset rack, a skill in its own device (§19.8).

  • The agent house holds who your agents are and how they work: an agent's own expression, its profile, the agent, its sessions, where it sits, its messages, and what it is trusted with.
  • The docs house is one device, Docs, whose rows are a project's account on six tiers, from its originating ground and intent, through the experience it means to give, its design, its architecture and its implementation, to its evidence and what came back (§16.1). A document's kind shows as a tag on its source, and the Document stays where you write it.
  • The workcell house is the road an agent's work travels, Gateway, Remote carrier, then Git / landing, with the machine, the seat, the checkouts and what a run leaves behind gathered onto it.

What lives outside the DLW comes in through an adapter, which keeps its own form and its function: your harnesses and their skills, your credentials, your other machines (§10.11). The day's NOWs, across your own ground, your projects and your workcells, can be looked over in one place, the NOWs widget: this machine's are read directly, another machine's by asking it.

The agent house and the docs house are different chains, and they meet only by reference. So "intent" has three homes. An agent's expression is the agent's. A task's intent is the task's, in its Intent panel. A project's originating intent is tier 0 of its Docs.

#10.5 The transport

The day opens and closes by itself. No hours are set in the instrument: Central keeps the day's bounds, and the transport and the Day show them. A run that should start by itself at a time is a routine in Settings (§10.10).

#10.6 Widgets

The rail on the right holds widgets: small live views of whatever you want to keep at hand while you work. Messages is the first: your agents and your groups, each with its conversation, so that talking to an agent is opening a tile and typing (§19.24). Beside it stand Epi and Nara, the DLW's own agents, as one widget that stays on the rail in every mode: Epi, the companion who works beside you and explains what you are looking at, and Nara, who answers from your own pages (§24). Their tile is an agent's tile (§19.4): the face of the one answering, its state, the last lines of the conversation and a composer. Choose Epi or Nara at its head, type, and press Enter. Others hold the packet, the trail, your agents at their stations, your workcells, a terminal, the files an agent is changing, the changes waiting for your approval, the wiki, the day's NOWs, the sky. Each widget holds a piece of context that belongs to your whole world, not to one kind of work, so it stays with you when you move. Open a terminal in Factory and it is still there in Central.

A widget is a device's view on the rail. A device that also stands on a chain opens from its tile into its other views. A monitor, such as Files or the Trail, has only its tile and its Full in a pane, where its settings stand across the head.

To open a widget, click its square in the launcher at the foot of the rail. To stop a widget following your selection, pin it. To widen the rail, drag its edge. To keep a group of widgets, save it as a preset.

Widgets are plugins. You can set each one up the way your work needs, and anyone can build new ones. To add a widget, install it from the browser's Devices.

#10.7 Going back

Every place you go is kept on the trail. To go back, press Back at the head of the title line, or select a stop on the Trail widget (§23.5). You return to the same place, the same page and the same point in the reading. Forward goes the other way, until you go somewhere new. Changing your kind of work never closes anything, and every place can be linked to and opened again.

#10.9 Acts and menus

Everything you can select acts as its counterpart in Live: a clip, an empty slot, a track, a row. Right-click it, or select it and press the menu key or ⇧F10, and its menu lists what you can do to it, each act with its key beside it. The same keys act on whatever is selected, and every act also has a home in the menu bar.

Object Its acts
Clip Launch (Enter) and Stop, in Session view. Cut (⌘X), Copy (⌘C), Duplicate (⌘D), Delete (⌫). Rename (⌘R), Switch off or on (0), Edit info text. In Arrangement view, Split (⌘E), Consolidate (⌘J) and Crop (⇧⌘J). In Central, Open and Reveal the page's file. Show in Browser, for a clip made of a constellation. A colour from Live's palette.
Empty slot Insert clip (⇧⌘M), Paste (⌘V), Record here on an armed track, Stop the track, Remove stop button (⌘E).
Track Rename (⌘R), Duplicate (⌘D), Delete (⌫). Switch off or on (0), Solo, Arm. Group (⌘G), Fold (U), Move left (⌘←) and right (⌘→). Retry, when its lane has stalled. In Central, Open and Reveal the world's folder. A colour.
Row Launch (Enter), Stop all clips. Insert row (⌘I), Rename (⌘R), Duplicate (⌘D), Delete (⌫).

Open hands a world's folder, or a page's file, to the application your computer opens it with, such as your editor. Reveal shows it in Finder. Neither changes the world: Central finds the folder among your work and asks the computer to open or show it.

What you do most often stands on the object itself: a clip's launch triangle, a slot's stop square, a track's switches. Everything else is in its menu. The menu bar holds every command once: Edit has Undo, Redo, Cut, Copy, Paste, Duplicate, Delete and Rename; Create has Insert Clip and Insert Row; View holds the views and the parts of the window (§10.1). Settings… stands in the application's menu, on ⌘,.

An act changes nothing itself. It asks the owner of what it changes: in Live, the set; in Central, the page and today's set in the Day; in Factory, the agent session and its tasks; in Expressions, the composition's scenes; in Technē, the reading. A clip's name, colour and switch go through its Clip view, which holds the revision the owner last gave; if Clip view is hidden, it comes forward first. The owner's answer, or its refusal in its own words, shows on the line under the grid or the ruler.

An act that its owner cannot take stays in the menu, dimmed. Point at it and the status bar says why: the operation it waits for, and whose. Delete and every other act that takes something away is drawn in the record colour, so it never looks like an act that cannot run. On a track read from another reading, each act that would change it says so instead.

Undo (⌘Z) takes back the last change an owner made through an act, and Redo (⇧⌘Z) makes it again. Each step is named as its act was, such as "Rename Bollingen", and undoes alone. Undo covers what owners keep: names, colours, switches. A fold, a view switched or a pane split is not a change to undo. While you type in a field, Undo and Redo are the field's own.

Where Live's keys would take a key the instrument already uses, the instrument keeps it. C turns a macro, and S plays a note of the Jankó keyboard, so Solo and Arm wait in the track's menu. U folds the selected group. 0 switches off what is selected; with nothing selected that can be switched off, it launches the tenth row.

#10.10 Settings

Product: O:I, holding the settings of every owner · Part of the window: a window of its own, on ⌘,

You need to change how your world works without hunting for each owner's files: what you have brought in, which harness and model a new conversation starts with, which keys reach which providers, which machines a workcell can carry work to, which verified Methods run by themselves, and how the window looks. Settings holds them in one window, after Live's: the pages down the left, the page you chose beside them. Each setting stays with its owner. Settings reads it from the owner, keeps your change local until you review it, and the owner applies it.

Settings is a window, as Live's is. It is not a device: it stands on no chain, in no pane and on no rail.

#The pages

Page What it holds Owner
Setup What you bring in: your ground, your harnesses and their skills, your credentials, your machines and your projects, each as found, with its preview and Accept (§10.11). Central, AIKit, Workcell
Harnesses & models The provider a new chat starts with, and the defaults for new sessions, such as the model each harness requests. Each harness client: installed, detected or why not, and what a change needs; Install, Folder and Sign in. The model routes of the catalogue, each with its standing: unproven, observed or usable. O:I's chat default, AIKit
Skills & methods The skill-sets offered by default, the capabilities composed into work, and each skill's standing. AIKit, Central
Profiles Your named profiles. Use stages a profile's settings as local changes; New from changes keeps your changes under a name; Import reads a profile file. The AIKit profile that composes new work. O:I, AIKit
Permissions The permission mode each harness starts in, and the owners' access policies, read only. Whether what you say to an agent may leave this machine: Local only, Ask or Allowed. AIKit, Central, Actuation
Credentials Each provider binding with its secret reference, its state and its last verdict, with Verify, Rotate and Revoke; Discover and Add binding. Workcell's secret references with what uses each, and its projections, with Scan and Revoke. AIKit, Workcell
Machines & services The remote machines a workcell can carry work to, each with its connection and what it was granted, with Connect, Disconnect and Remove; Add machine. The services the workcell declares and the local services AIKit elects. Workcell, AIKit
Automations Routines: verified Methods that run on a schedule or an event, each with its state, its next run and whether it runs unattended, with Enable, Run now, Disable and Reprove; Create routine. The Methods you can make a routine from, the harness timers not yet adopted, and the run history. This is the one place a run is given a time: no device and no pad keeps one. AIKit
Search & telemetry Factory's search limits and its watch interval. Factory
Sources & libraries The Central project each register binds to. Factory
Appearance Light, Dark or Follow system, or a library theme, with Apply and Revert; the themes you imported, with Import and Remove; the visual layer and the welcome scene. O:I's presentation
Products & updates Each of the six products with its version and its state. The desktop is a full install: every product comes with it, and none is added or removed here. The one you choose shows what is degraded and why, and what it still owes. Under them, the installation's own details. Each product
System Each owner's System reading on four axes, declared, effective, active and staged, with the drift between two of them; or the owners' read-only configuration. Each product

Skills & methods, Permissions, Search & telemetry and Sources & libraries show only when an owner contributes a setting to them.

#A setting's row

Every setting an owner contributes stands as one row: its name and owner, its value, where the value comes from, and when a change takes effect.

Column What it shows
Value The value in effect, as the control you change it with: a chooser, a switch or a field. A list or a table opens its entries under the row. A secret shows its reference, never the key.
From This scope, where the value is set here; inherited, where the owner resolves it from a wider scope or its default.
Applies When a change takes effect: at the next resolution, for new sessions, on reconnect or on restart. Read only, where the owner lets nothing change it.
Reset Removes this scope's value, and the owner resolves it again. It stands where this scope sets the value.

A change is local until you review it. Its row carries an amber mark, the page's name counts its changes, and the foot of the window counts them all. Review changes asks each owner to plan your changes. The Review page lists each plan with its scope, the change and when it applies, and Apply sends the plans the owners made. Each owner answers in the same table: applied, verified or refused, with its reason. When an owner's reading moves under a change you made, Keep holds your change on the new reading. Discard drops every change.

#Controls

Control Values Default What it does
Search Text Empty Finds pages, settings, and the settings that stand beside an instrument. Press a result to go to it.
Applies to This machine · World · a project · a workcell This machine The scope the owners' settings are read and changed at.
Show Routines · Methods · Timers · History Routines What the Automations page lists.
Work context This AIKit home · a project This AIKit home Where the Automations page reads routines and makes them.
System Four axes · Configuration, and an owner Four axes What the System page shows, and whose reading.

#The window

A head holds Search and the owners' connection; the pages stand down the left and the page beside them; a foot holds your local changes, Discard and Review changes. Nothing in the window scrolls: a long list turns its pages with ‹ and ›.

#Transport

The transport does not reach Settings. A setting changes what starts next: a running session keeps its harness, its model and its composition.

#To use Settings

  1. Press ⌘, or choose Settings… in the application's menu.
  2. Choose a page down the left, or type in Search and press a result.
  3. Set Applies to, then change a value. Its row takes an amber mark.
  4. Press Review changes… and read each owner's plan.
  5. Press Apply, and read each owner's answer in the table.
  6. Press Esc to go back to the work you came from.

#Rules

  • Settings shows no secret. A credential, a projection and a machine's connection show their reference. A key you enter goes to the computer's own secure field and on to the credential owner, never through the window.
  • A page shows each setting as a row with its control. An owner's raw record never stands on a page; its configuration as written stands read only on the System page.
  • Where a harness or a provider has a login of its own, Sign in runs it in a terminal, where you answer it, and the page reads the result back. It stands on each harness client on Harnesses & models, and beside a provider's key on Credentials. A harness that signs in only inside itself says so in its own words and offers no button, and a login the page cannot read affects that harness alone.
  • A change stays yours until its owner applies it.
  • An act its owner cannot take stays in place, dimmed, and the status bar says why.
  • A setting that belongs beside an instrument, such as a device's parameter, opens there. Search finds it.
  • Discover and Scan report where a key lies, never what it holds. Neither changes a setting.
  • Revoke, Remove, Disconnect, Run now and Disable are held: press and hold them.
