  • A run that starts by itself at a time is a routine on the Automations page. No device, pad or Day move keeps a time of its own.

#Tips

  • To start a building day with the same defaults, keep them as a profile and press Use.
  • To see why a workcell does not hold what it declares, open System and read the drift column.
  • To find a setting fast, press ⌘, then ⌘F and type a word of its name.

#10.11 Bringing in what you have

You need to start from the work and the tools you already have, keep them working as they did, and add only what helps. The first time you open the DLW, Settings opens on its Setup page, over Central, which stands on today's Day and a Flow in Pane view (§18.1). After that the DLW opens on the world you chose, in the mode and the view you left. Setup reads your computer and goes through five steps in order. Each step shows what it found, previews every change it would make, and makes them only when you press Accept, which is held. Until then nothing you have moves or changes.

Step What setup finds What Accept does Where you come back to it
Ground Where your own ground lies, or that you have none yet. Adopts the ground where it is, or makes a new one in the folder you choose, under the name you give it. Nothing in an adopted ground moves. Settings, Setup
Harnesses and skills Each agent tool you use, with its settings, its instructions and its skills. A tool or a setting setup cannot read is named and left alone. Connects each tool through its adapter, so its skills keep their function in the DLW and in the tool itself. The tool's own settings and plugins stay as they are. Settings, Harnesses & models and Skills & methods
Credentials Where each provider's key lies: the place, never the value. Binds each key by reference. The value stays in your computer's secure store; the DLW never shows it and never keeps it. Settings, Credentials
Machines This computer, and the other machines you reach. Makes this computer a workcell, and prepares another machine as a place to work, keeping its own settings. Settings, Machines & services; the browser's Machines
Projects Your folders of work, inside your ground's Work or anywhere else, and any wiki a folder already keeps. Adopts a project where it stands, or migrates it into your ground's Work under its own name, with its ProjectCentral beside its material. A wiki is kept in place or copied in, as you choose; where a folder holds two, you choose which. A migrated project's original stays until you remove it. The browser's Work place: Add folder… opens this step for that folder

Your world is one folder, which you choose and name in the Ground step. Every product keeps your world's state in that folder, and the DLW opens the world you chose. My World stands on it in the browser's You place.

Once your ground is made, Setup asks for your date of birth. It is the first layer of Nara's identity, so that you are represented in your world beside your projects. It is kept in your ground, and your Being page holds it by reference (§24.6). Leave it, and it stays absent until you give it; nothing fills it in your place.

A project you have brought in is a world in the browser's Work place. To work in it today, drag it onto an empty track in Central: as in Live, a drop on a track admits what you dropped into the set. Dropping a folder on a track never sets it up.

Setup asks only for what your first useful task needs, and what you leave out is not shown as missing. Stop it halfway and what you accepted stays; run it again and nothing is made twice. Run it over an older setup and it brings the setup into agreement, keeping your local edits beside what it proposes. The desktop is a full install: every product it carries is there from the first open, and Setup adds none and removes none (§10.10).

You can also come in without the window, from the coding tool you already talk to. Paste the adoption request into that conversation. The agent reads what you have, and before it changes anything tells you what it found and what each addition would do for you: one door to the products, a ground for your work, agents whose acts are their own and bounded, and the practice and context your tools receive. Take all of it, keep what you have, or take less. If the conversation cannot run commands on your computer, the agent gives you the exact step to take, and never says your computer changed when it did not. When it is done it tells you what is active now and what waits for a reload, a new session or a restart, and how to carry on; it never restarts your tool to make a check pass. Then it helps you with a piece of your own work, so you see the result, and says which harness and model did the work, what practice they received, what changed and where it lies. You can go on in that tool and open the same work in the DLW later: neither door is needed for the other.

#The Projects step

Setup reads a folder and says what it found. It draws the folder with its own material at the left and ProjectCentral at the right, its parts dashed where they would be made.

Central finds What you can do
No wiki Create: ProjectCentral is made around the folder. Nothing in the folder moves.
One wiki Keep in place: the wiki stays where it is and joins the world's wiki as one of its sources. Copy in: the wiki is copied into ProjectCentral, and the original stays where it was.
More than one wiki Choose the wiki, then keep it in place or copy it in. Central does not choose for you.
A ProjectCentral it cannot read Nothing here. Mend its manifest by hand.
The ground in place Nothing to make.
Control What it does
Make Create, Keep in place or Copy in. A choice the folder does not allow stays closed and says why.
Wiki The folder's wiki to keep or copy.
Preview Lists every step Central would take, in order. Nothing changes.
Accept Makes the world's ground as previewed. It is held.

#Rules

  • Nothing you have moves, changes or is deleted before you accept.
  • A key's value is never shown and never kept.
  • What setup cannot read is named and kept as it was.
  • Accept and Remove are held.

#Part Two — The Game

#11. The figure

The game began, Hesse tells us, on a frame like a child's abacus. A musicologist strung glass beads of different sizes and colours along its wires, and the wires stood for the lines of a stave, so that he could set out a theme in beads, transpose it, develop it, and play one theme against another. Within a few generations the beads were gone. What remained was a language in which mathematics and music counted equally, where a Bach fugue, a law of nature and a saying of Confucius could stand in the same sentence. Hesse's narrator calls it "a mode of playing with the total contents and values of our culture," and says its player plays "like the organist on an organ."

Hesse wrote around the rules rather than writing them down, but he lets us watch a game closely enough to follow it. A master sets a symbol before the players. Each of them stops and considers it in silence — what it holds, where it came from, what it means — so that the sign will not go empty. Then the theme is worked against others, the way a fugue works its subject. New symbols enter the game's archive rarely, through one competition a year. Great games run for days, under rules strict enough to say how long the players may sleep, and private games are played by anyone who wants to play one. Every game is written down so that it can be read back. And the master who has given his life to it knows that it will end; beauty, once it has entered history, passes.

Nobody built it. For most of a century the Glass Bead Game was the closest picture we had of a whole environment for meaning, and it stayed a picture. Then music, the art Hesse had taken for his model, got the environment he imagined. Live put composition, sound design, recording, mixing and performance in one place with one clock, and anyone could sit down at it.

The DLW takes the step from there to what Hesse described: Live's grammar, pointed at the contents of a world. Its centre is an instrument, as it should be. Hesse's game grew from a bead frame strung like a stave. The DLW grows from a torus whose keys are points along its helices, and whose chords draw the symbols they belong to. Here, as in Hesse's novel, the language of symbols and the language of sound are one language.

#12. The game's language

In Hesse's game the player was never only moving symbols about. Each theme was a piece of the world's knowledge, and each move worked on the player as well. Knecht describes a game well played closing around the one who played it the way a sphere closes around its centre, so that they came away having taken a whole, ordered world into themselves. The DLW is built for that double movement. What you make in your world becomes knowledge others can walk through, and making it is how you come to know. Take either half away and the other goes hollow.

You develop a theme by carrying it. You meet it in the day's work, take it into a scene until you can hear what it is, and lay it along a walk that someone else can follow. Each step changes its form, and each step asks something different of you.

Hesse's players knew two schools. One found the game's unity in the material, in how the themes fitted together. The other found it in the player, in a sequence of meditations that led them, move by move, towards experiencing the whole. One school faces the world and the other faces the self, and the DLW keeps room for both. In Technē you work the material until it holds: the history checked, the relations accepted, the palace built room by room. In Expressions you meet the same material as something lived, a field you stand inside and listen to.

At the great public games, what the people watching valued most was the silence. After each symbol every player stopped and considered it — what it held, where it came from, what it meant — so that the sign would stay full. The DLW gives that silence its place in Expressions, where a presence meets you in the field, listens, answers, and never judges. Hesse's game required the pause; the instrument does not. Nara's phenomenological, dialogical and meditative techniques carry the meditative side (§24), and nothing automatic fills the silence.

Any game could be read back into the disciplines it was made from. Knecht spent years translating a single school game, phrase by phrase, into mathematics, ornament, Chinese and Greek. Every reference in the DLW keeps its owner and its version so that you can do the same: follow anything back to where it began. Jean Gebser called that beginning the ever-present origin, a source that stays present rather than receding into the past. Tracing it is a kind of care, and it runs in both directions: back through what a thing came from, and back through what you came from in coming to know it.

Magister Ludi first meant simply schoolmaster, and Knecht ends his life as a teacher. The DLW teaches the way any instrument does. A companion works beside you and explains what you are looking at, and the rest you learn by playing.

Hesse gave his players a village. The DLW gives them a field. Every player is a world in it, every visit lands on what its host has chosen to show, and every gift arrives under its giver's name. He kept the private game as well — "to this day everyone is free to play the Game privately" — and your world, before you have shown any of it, is where that game is played.

Games were written down so they could be played again. Here a day closes into what it taught, a walk is recorded, a take is kept, and whoever you give them to can play them in their own world.

And games end. A day in the DLW closes by itself.

#13. Epi-Logos

In Hesse's novel the game belonged to an Order. Scholars who had given their lives to it played it in a closed province, and everyone else came only as guests. Epi-Logos is that game opened to anyone: the Glass Bead Game played with what we now know, by whoever sits down to play.

Take one move. Pythagoras taught that all is number. The Gospel of John opens with the Word. Much later a psychologist and a physicist, Jung and Pauli, wrote to each other for a quarter of a century and came to think that number was the oldest ordering of all, older than the split between mind and matter. Set the three side by side and none of them has to give way: the number that orders, the word that names, and the place the two scientists found where they meet. A player who can hold all three and show how each answers the others has made a move. Hesse's players made the same kind of move with a fugue and a law of nature.

Moves are played on a map. Picture Spinoza's Ethics, set out in geometric order with every proof citing the proofs it stands on, and then picture it alive, so that you can question it. Each idea has an address, each relation a path you can walk, each claim a way back to its source, and everyone who plays adds to it. Most maps stand outside the land they show. This one maps awareness, and nobody can stand outside that, so the map holds the person reading it. You are on it.

The game carries a story about language. Words once acted on the world: a name could call, a spell could bind. Each age since has made words more exact and less alive, until in ours they mostly label what instruments measure. The story ends where we are now, with machines built out of language, and asks whether they could help bring back what was lost — the sense of living inside what we name.

So players dig into words. Every word holds a record of how people have tried to name what is real. Whole, health and holy grow from one root, and you can follow that root down until the three stand together again.

Jung and Pauli also dreamed of a clock of the world, one that would tell the state of meaning rather than the hour. The sky over your planet is the game's attempt to build it. The planets stand where they really stand, and the torus at the centre turns with them. On a day you can't account for, look up, and see where everything stood while you lived it.

None of it counts unless it changes the player. Jung called that change individuation: becoming who you already are. The philosophers of Kashmir called it recognition: finding that what you are was never missing. One path runs inward and the other outward, and Epi-Logos wagers that they meet. A child's taunt says it best. It takes one to know one.

That change is practised in Nara, a world of your own that nobody else can see into. Say a decision has stayed with you for a month. On the first morning you opened it as a concern to carry, and drew three cards. Since then you have written beside them, dreamt twice about the house in question, and sat with it most evenings. Nara has read all of it as you wrote it. Ask it now and it answers from those pages, naming each passage it used. The cards are still where they fell, and the I Ching shows how the question has turned.

The machines have work in the game too. They are made of words carried on numbers, so they can read back over everything we have written and help find what it means. They read, gather, propose and build, and they defer — to what they cannot know, and to the person they work for. An agent can hand a decision up. It cannot approve its own work.

The Truth's as much what ever was As what's ever anew.

#14. What the game warns

Hesse wrote the game's decline into its history, and three of his warnings apply to anything built in its image.

A form can grow more beautiful than what it carries, and then it is glass. The DLW meets that by asking of every part what work it does in a real day: whatever cannot do its part is ornament.

A device that judges for the player — scores the scene, picks the reading — takes the silence away. The DLW's companions answer and explain; you decide.

Analysis can outlive the music it studied. The close study of Live serves an instrument that sounds, or it has lost its point.

The test of the whole is what people leave with: a day closed into what it taught, work landed, an expression shown, a reader who understood, a pupil who no longer needs the teacher. Hesse's novel ends with its Magister leaving the Order to teach a single pupil.

#Part Three — The catalogue

#16. How devices work

You play a device while your attention is on the material. The agent runs, the field moves, the torus rings, and your eyes are there, not on the device. So a device must show its state at a glance, answer the hand at once, and never ask you to read. Live solved this. Every Live device is one panel of one height: a picture of what the device does, with handles on it, and the controls set round the picture. You learn one panel and you can read all of them. The DLW draws every device the same way.

Live's chains hold three kinds of device, and so do the DLW's. An instrument makes something. An agent answers, the field moves and sounds, the world draws its places, the journey walks its stops, the Day gathers the day, the torus rings. An effect changes what passes through it and keeps the rest: a scope limits what an agent may touch, a filter shapes the torus, the packet gathers what an agent will read. A rack holds several chains under one device: the skills an agent may use, the agents of a team, the field devices of the Studio.

Three more kinds work beside the chains. A modulator moves the settings of other devices from a source of its own and never touches the material, as Live's LFO does. A monitor shows what is happening and what has happened, as Live's Spectrum and MIDI monitor do, and writes nothing. A connection brings agents to the work and takes their work to where it lands, as Live's audio interface carries sound in and out of every track.

#What each part keeps

Every device, view and control takes one of Live's meanings and keeps what makes it that thing (§3). What it must keep follows from what it is:

It is It keeps
An instrument It names the act of its owner that makes the material.
An effect It names the material it works on, changes what passes through it and keeps the rest. It never replaces the material without leaving a receipt.
A rack It holds at least one chain, and a way to choose between its chains.
A macro It turns at least one real setting of its own device, each within that setting's range.
A track It names the stream it carries, and keeps no copy of it.
A clip It holds its material by reference and version, and shows its state.
A stop It names the clips it stands together.

Each device declares which of Live's meanings it takes. A device that declares none, or declares one it does not keep, is refused when it is brought in, and the refusal names what it lacks. Where Live has the same object, the device names Live's, so that what it does can be checked against what Live does.

The grammar does not change from mode to mode; what it means does. The same slots of the transport, the same views, the same chain and the same browser serve every mode; what each one does is the mode's, set out in the transport's table (§10.5) and in each mode's section. A device opened in another mode keeps every control it has and works on that mode's material.

Owners write, and devices read. A parameter that its owner can change carries the way the change reaches the owner; a parameter without one is a reading, and its control only shows (§16.13). The shell keeps no copy of what an owner keeps. Nothing moves without a cause you can see: a value that something else moves names what moved it (§16.11).

#Rules for every device and view

These hold for every device, every view and every state the window can be in.

  • Things that look alike are kept apart. Reading a thing is not acting on it, and seeing an act is not being allowed to take it. Selecting a thing does not give it to an agent, and being present is not being allowed. A thing hidden from you is not missing, and a thing degraded is not broken. What you wrote, what was observed and what was generated stay marked apart. What a world shows, what someone offers it and the source itself are three things. Who takes part is not who someone is, and meeting a claim is not believing it. A receipt does not mean you have seen or accepted what it records, and what is carried to an agent is not what it has loaded.
  • What a thing is belongs to its owner, and how it is shown belongs to the window. Neither is worked out from the other: a layout never changes what a page says, and a change to the page never moves the panes. A draft you are writing stays in your hands until its owner acknowledges the save.
  • When something is missing, slow or failing, the window says so where the thing would stand: what is missing, whose it is, and what can bring it back. It never shows an empty success in its place, and it never holds the whole window waiting. A view that shows only part of something says how much it leaves out.
  • Whatever asks for your attention names exactly what it is about, and one act takes you there. An ordinary wait, or a reading going by, does not ask for your attention.
  • Nothing that arrives takes your focus. A message, a run's progress or a returned result shows where it belongs and waits there: it does not change what you have selected, rearrange your panes or open a part you have hidden. Only a tile or a view you have set to Follow keeps up with it.
  • An agent is shown everything it is allowed to know, whole. You are shown the same facts, opening further as you go into them. Being an agent never widens what is shown.
  • Whatever you can do with the pointer you can do from the keyboard, and whatever you can do from the keyboard you can do with the pointer.

#16.1 What goes where

A device is one kind of thing among five, and most of what the DLW does belongs to one of the other four. Live draws the lines, and the DLW keeps them.

Thing What it is What belongs to it
Track One stream of material, and the chain that works on it. Its name, colour, the I/O of its work, its mixer row, and its chain. In Central a world; in Factory a session; in Expressions an Expression; in Technē a reading; in Live a part.
Clip A piece of the material on a track. Its name, colour and length, the constellation it comes from, how it launches and what follows it, and its content. Everything that changes the clip itself belongs here: a highlight on a page, a symbol's place in a scene, a task's instruction.
Clip view The clip's editor, in the detail area. Panels after Live's: Clip, Launch, the editor, and Envelopes. What each mode's editor holds is in §16.5.
Device Works on the material as it passes along the chain. What changes how the material sounds, looks or acts, without rewriting the clip, for every clip on the track.
View A way of seeing tracks and clips. Session view's grid, Arrangement view's ruler with its lanes and takes, the panes of Pane view, the widget rail.

So a capability lives in one place:

  • A thing that edits the clip is a tool of its editor. Text, Highlight and Notes shape and mark the page you are writing. They are the editing tools of a Central page in Clip view, as Live's note tools are, and the passage acts in the page reach them. A selected symbol's force, form, voice and meaning are the selected object's controls in the scene's editor.
  • One job is one device, in every mode. The agent that answers in a Central page and the agent that runs a Factory task is one Agent (§19.4): who it is, how it works, how much it decides alone, and its thread. What an agent may read and where it may write is one Scope (§19.12), with its Knowledge page inside it, on any track an agent works on.
  • How a write arrives is set in two places only. Scope sets the most an agent may do in each part of the world: propose, draft or write. Arm, in the transport, lets the agents of a track write directly with receipts or keeps them proposing. Every proposal waits in Approvals on the Main track, and in the page or scene it belongs to.
  • A widget is a device's view on the rail. The packet and the approvals on the rail are the widget views of devices that stand on chains, and an agent's tile is its conversation in Messages. A monitor, such as Files or the Ledger, stands only on the rail and in a pane, and has only those two views (§16.3).
  • Where an agent works is set once. The gateway an agent reaches its harness through, the machine that carries it, the seat it changes and how its work lands make up a workcell's chain. The machine's own state, the seats and checkouts, and what a run leaves behind are pages of that chain's devices, not devices of their own. A track names its workcell in its In/Out section, so every agent on the track, in every mode, works through the same chain (§16.6, §19.23).
  • The views are not devices. Session view and Arrangement view are two views of the mode's one set of tracks, and Pane view holds the Full views of devices beside them (§10.2). No pane holds Session view or Arrangement view. The course of a run is its track in Arrangement view; its attempts are takes; a task is a clip. Technē's timeline is Arrangement view, not an instrument of its own.
  • A device is never a track. A device stands on a chain, in a pane or on the rail. It is never drawn as a track, and a track's own settings stand on its head and its mixer row, never on a device's page.
  • Settings is a window. It holds what owners let you set (§10.10). It is not a device and stands on no chain.
  • A corpus is material, not an instrument. A body of work such as the Return of Zero or the Quaternal Logic is read, walked and played through the universal instruments, the world, the journey, the palace and the graph, and along Arrangement view's ruler. A device a corpus brings, such as the Deck or the M3 clock, reads its material, and sits on a reading's chain like any other.

#Six kinds of device

Every device does one of six kinds of work. Its kind says where it stands, which views it has (§16.3), and whose time it keeps.

Kind What it does Where it stands Whose time it keeps For example
Instrument Makes the material of a track. At the head of a track's chain, and full in a pane. A few are born in a pane or on the rail, and stand only there. The transport's. Play starts it, Stop stops it, and Record keeps what it made as a take. Agent, Field, Torus, World, Document, Day; born on the rail, Messages and Terminal
Effect Changes what passes through it and keeps the rest. On a chain, after the instrument. Its track's. Scope, Packet, Physics, Exact-ratio tuning, Approvals
Rack Holds chains side by side, with macros that reach into them. On a chain. Its chains'. Skillset rack, Agentset rack, Studio
Modulator Moves settings of other devices from a source of its own, and never touches the material. On any chain. It moves settings on any track, in any mode, and each setting it moves names it. Its own clock: the sky of now, or of a chosen day. It keeps moving while the transport stands. Sky modulation; a clip's Modulation envelope (§16.5)
Monitor Shows what is happening and what has happened, and opens what it shows. It writes nothing. On the rail, and full in a pane. Never on a chain. The present. Follow keeps it there; scroll back and it reads the record. In Arrangement view the same events lie along a track's event lanes. Files, Trail, NOWs, Web, Wiki, Ledger
Connection Brings agents to the work, and takes their work to where it lands. On a workcell's chain; Link stands in the transport. Never on a track's chain. Its own. It stays up whether or not the transport plays, and its heartbeat is the agents' check-in. Gateway, Remote carrier, Git / landing with its Seat, Link

Between them the monitors keep what is live in front of you: your own trail, your agents' messages and the frames they send, the files and changes they make, the receipts their writes leave, and the day's NOWs.

#How the kinds work together

Material runs one way, from the instrument through the effects, left to right. A rack's macros reach into its chains. A modulator reaches across tracks and modes to the settings it moves; take hold of one and the modulator lets go of it until you press Re-enable. A connection carries an agent in and its work out, and what it carries is what the monitors read: the frames that cross a gateway, the files a seat changes, the receipts a landing leaves. Press what a monitor shows and it opens, in the monitor's Full or in the instrument it belongs to. Every proposal, whichever device made it, waits in Approvals.

#How far a setting reaches

A setting made on Holds for
A clip, in Clip view That clip.
A device on a track's chain Every clip on that track.
The Main track Every track of the mode's set.
A workcell Every agent that works in it, on any track, in every mode.
The transport, the rail and the browser Your whole world, in every mode.

#Live's acts, kept as Live keeps them

A Live object borrowed by the DLW keeps what it does in Live. Where a function is not that act, it has its own home.

Live's Does in the DLW Is never
Track activator The track plays, or it does not. Off, the track is silent and dimmed, and keeps its place and its settings. Where the work goes: that is the track's Output, as whether a world sends to the Day. What you watch of it: that is its Monitor. Showing or hiding.
Solo You attend to the soloed tracks alone: you see and hear only them, in the views and the instruments. The others keep running. A limit on what may run.
Loop Whether a clip repeats, set in its Clip panel with its start and end. The transport's loop repeats the stretch of the ruler under the brace. A launch mode. Launch modes are Live's: Trigger, Gate, Toggle and Repeat.
Follow action What comes after a clip, on the clip's own track. A move to another track.
Punch in and out Where recording, and in Factory an agent's writing, may happen on the ruler. A clock time.
Pad Triggers: pressed, it plays now, as a Drum Rack pad does. A schedule. When something happens later belongs to the ruler, to an automation lane, or to a routine in Settings, Automations (§10.10).
A drop on an empty track Starts a track with what you dropped, or admits material into the set. How something is set up. Setup is its own act (§10.11).
Return track A chain that several tracks share. In Factory, a workcell. A device drawn as a track: what it carries stands on its chain.
Settings A window of its own, on ⌘,. A device, a pane or a widget.

#Houses and their chains

Devices that serve one concern stand together as a house (§10.4). Three houses hold most of what is not a track's material, and each runs along a chain of its own.

House Its chain What stands in it Making one
Agent The agency chain: an agent's expression, its profile, the agent, its session, where it sits, its messages, what it is trusted with. The Agent, with its skills and scope on a session's chain; Messages on the rail; the Agentset rack for a group; the Skillset rack and the skill's own device. Using the Agent, the Agentset rack or the skill's device on something new.
Docs The documentation chain: a project's account on six tiers, 0 its originating ground and intent, 1 the experience it means to give, 2 its design, 3 its architecture, 4 its implementation, 5 its evidence and returns. Docs, one device on a world's chain, whose rows are the six tiers. A document's kind is a tag on its source. The Document is the editor (§17.8). Opening the Document from a tier's row.
Workcell The workcell chain: Gateway, Remote carrier, Git / landing with its Seat. The machine the work runs on, its seats and checkouts, and what a run leaves behind, as pages of those devices (§19.23). Using those devices on a new machine or seat.

The chains are different things and join only by reference: a session names the workcell it works in; a task's intent names the source it comes from in Docs; what an agent lands returns as evidence to tier 5. "Intent" has three homes: an agent's expression in the agency chain, a task's intent in its Intent panel, and a project's origin at tier 0 of Docs.

Harnesses and their skills, credentials and other machines come in through adapters, which keep each thing's own form and its function, and leave a reference in the DLW (§10.11).

#16.2 Chains on tracks

A track holds one stream of material. Its chain holds the devices that the material passes through, from left to right.

Mode Track Chain, left to right
Central A world. The set is the Day; its die is on the Main track. The packet, the agent of the world, and its scope; then Docs, the world's account on six tiers. On the Main track: the Day, then Approvals.
Factory An agent session. Agent, skills rack, scope. On the Main track: the Run map, Approvals and the prompt pads.
Expressions An Expression. The Studio: the field, then its field devices.
Technē A reading. The instrument it plays through, then the Lens and the other effects that read it.
Live A part. The note devices, the torus, then its effects.

A workcell has a chain of its own: its Gateway, the Remote carrier that names the machine it runs on, and Git / landing with the Seat inside it (§19.23). Every track that works in the workcell shares that chain, as Live's tracks share a return track's chain. What the machine holds against what you declared for it, the seats and their checkouts, and what a run leaves behind are pages of these three devices.

A device is not tied to a mode. It goes wherever its material is. An agent and its skills work on a Central page as well as on a Factory session. The world draws any track that has places. The sky can move a parameter in any mode.

#16.3 Six views

A device has one set of values and up to six views. It has the views of the places it stands in, and a change in one view shows in the others at once.

View Where What it holds Live's nearest
Folded The chain The activator, the name and up to two short readings, read downward, in a strip 22 px wide. A folded device.
Compact The chain The display and up to four macros, at the chain's height. The width comes from the sections. The device on its chain; a rack with only its macros showing.
Whole Expanded above the chain Every parameter, grouped, and the display with all its handles, in a band as wide as the detail area: the bands stand side by side and the display grows into the room. The expanded view of EQ Eight or Wavetable.
Full A pane, in Pane view The material itself: the page, the field, the torus, the world. No controls. A rack's material is its devices: its Full holds every device of its chains in its Whole view, with every setting live. Wavetable's large display, without its controls. For a rack, the rack with every chain and device shown.
Pop-out Its own window, which can fill the screen The material with every control docked under it. A plug-in's window.
Widget The rail A small display and up to three readings or macros, in a tile of 136 × 136 px or 280 × 136 px. Live has none. Push's display is the nearest.
A device that stands Has these views
On a chain: an instrument, an effect, a rack, a modulator, or a connection on its workcell's chain Folded, Compact and Whole
In a pane, with material of its own Full, and Pop-out for its own window
On the rail Widget
On the rail and in a pane only: a monitor, or an instrument born there Widget and Full. Its window holds its Full.

A monitor has nothing to fold or to expand over a chain, so it has two views. Its tile holds its live display, with its main setting as a handle on the display. Its Full holds everything it shows, with every setting it has in one line across the head of the pane.

  • Whole stands in one place, its band above the chain. A device you have not put on a chain has no Whole: select it in the browser to read what it does.
  • Most devices need no pop-out of their own. The window shows Full above and Whole below it. A device writes its own only where its controls belong beside the material rather than under it.
  • A pane holds no device controls. They stay in Device view under the pane, or in the device's window. Two kinds stand otherwise. A rack's Full holds controls, because its material is its devices: the same devices, with the same values, as on its chain, and its macros stand at its head. A monitor has no Device view, so its settings stand in the head of its pane.

#16.4 Opening, folding and hiding

The window is modular: every part opens, folds and hides, and the other parts take the space.

A device's head reads as Live's does, from the left:

Part Does
Activator Asks the owner to turn the device on or off. The light shows what the owner reports.
▸ Expanded view Shows the device's expanded view: Whole, as a band above the chain. ▾ while it stands; press it again to hide it.
Name Double-click the head to fold the device to its title, or choose Fold from its context menu. Press the folded title to open it again.
Rail, ▦ Pane, ↗ Pop out At the right. Keep the device on the widget rail; open it full in the pane that has focus; open it in its own window. Press ↗ in the window to close it.

Press the plate to select the device: the keys and the status bar speak to it. Right-click the head for Fold, Rename, Group, Save as preset, Hot-swap, Show automation and Map. A rack's head has three more marks, as Live's do: show or hide the macros, the chain list, and the devices of the selected chain.

The expanded view is a band as wide as the detail area, between Clip view and the chain. The panes above it shrink to make room; nothing is covered. One device stands expanded at a time, and it stays on the chain under its band. Any number of windows can stay open. A window follows its device: when the device leaves the chain, its window closes.

The detail area holds Clip view above Device view, both at once when there is room, as Live 12 does. Hide either one, or switch between them when only one shows.

To show or hide Do
The detail area ⌥⌘L, or ▲ beside Clip and Device at the bottom right.
Clip view or Device view ⌥⌘3 or ⌥⌘4, or ▲ beside its switch at the bottom right. ⇧Tab switches between them when only one shows.
Clip view in the main area ⌥⌘E. The clip's editor takes the main area; press again to return.
The browser ⌥⌘B or ⌥⌘5.
The pool ⌥⌘6, as Live shows its Groove Pool. Drag the line between the browser and the pool to give either the height.
The widget rail ⌥⌘8, or its toggle at the top right. Drag its edge to widen it. Fold the launcher to give the tiles the height.
The mixer ⌥⌘M, or Mixer at the bottom right.
A device's expanded view ▸ on its head, or Esc.
A device's window ↗ on its head, or the window's own close.

#16.5 Clip view and Device view

Select a clip and the detail area shows it. Clip view shows the clip and its editor. Device view shows the chain of the clip's track.

Clip view is laid out as Live lays it out, in every mode. Only what each part holds changes with the kind of clip.

Part Where What it holds Live's
Head Across the top The clip's activator, its name on its colour. The clip's title bar.
Clip The first panel, first tab The constellation the clip comes from, where the clip starts and ends, whether it loops, its length, its signature, its groove and its scale, and the facts that belong to the clip alone. The sample, Start, End, Loop, Position, Length, Signature, Groove, Scale.
Launch The first panel, second tab How the clip launches, when the launch lands, and what follows it, with what chance. Launch mode, Legato, Quantize, Velocity, Follow Action.
Tools The second panel, in tabs Tools that change the clip's content as a whole. A transform reshapes what is there; a generator proposes new content. A tool shows its few controls and one button that applies it, or applies as you turn it. Pitch and Time, Transform, Generate.
Editor The rest of the area, in tabs The content itself. The first tab is the clip's own material. Envelopes moves a parameter over the clip's own time. A third tab holds what each element of the content carries on its own, lane by lane. Notes or Sample, Envelopes, MPE.
  • A clip's source is its constellation, as a sample is an audio clip's. The Clip panel names it under Constellation, in every mode, and Show in Browser beside it selects it in the browser (§10.3). An edit changes the clip, never the constellation, and never another mode's clip of the same constellation.
  • Groove, in the Clip panel, chooses a QL frame or an MEF lens from the pool, as Live's chooses a groove; in Live it also offers the set's grooves. Hot-swap tries another while the clip plays. The clip is read through what you choose, and its source stays as it is (§16.7).
  • The editor folds and highlights as Live's does: Fold keeps only the rows that hold content, and a scale or a set of kinds highlights what belongs.
  • An envelope picks its device and its parameter. On a device's parameter it is Automation, which sets the value over the clip, or Modulation, which moves the track's own value up and down. Linked, it runs with the clip; unlinked, it has its own length and loop.
  • A clip on Arrangement view's ruler has no Launch tab, as in Live. A clip that is placed rather than launched, such as a Central page, never has one.
  • Whether a clip repeats is its Loop, in the Clip tab. Launch holds Live's launch modes, Trigger, Gate, Toggle and Repeat, and a follow action that stays on the clip's own track.
  • A change in the editor changes the clip. A device on the chain changes what passes through it and leaves the clip as it is (§16.1).
  • What a clip lacks, Clip view leaves out.
Mode The clip Its editor's tabs Launch Envelopes
Technē (§17.1) An event or a walk's stop Material, Relations, Constellation, Source Arrival, and the walk's next stop None
Central (§18.1) A page Page and Source; a Flow's Dialogue, Flow and Journal None None
Factory (§19.1) A task The log Launch mode, Quantize, the follow action The Agent's Effort and Autonomy for this task
Expressions (§20.1) A scene Sequence, Envelopes, Expression, Sound Quantize, the next scene, Jump The scene's automation
Live (§21.1) A note clip or an audio clip Notes, Envelopes, MPE; or Sample, Envelopes Live's own Live's own

#Clip view and Device view side by side

Clip view Device view
For Changing the selected clip itself: its content, where it starts and ends, and how it launches. Shaping what works on a track's material, for every clip on the track, without changing any clip.
What it acts on The selected clip. The chain of the selected track, or of the device in the focused pane.
What you do there Edit the content, set the clip's facts, apply a tool, draw an envelope. Turn a device's controls; add, move and remove devices; open a device's expanded view.
Selecting Select inside the editor: a note, a passage, a step. Click a device's plate.
Focus ⌥3, and ⌥8 for the selected panel. ⌥4
Its forms Under the main area, or above Device view when both show; or filling the main area with ⌥⌘E. Under Clip view, or alone; with one device standing expanded as a band above the chain.
While it loads The clip's last content stands at once, dimmed until its owner answers. Each device shows its last picture, dimmed until its owner answers.
Empty With no clip selected, Clip view stands empty. An empty chain waits for a device from the browser.
Switched off A deactivated clip shows grey, and you can still edit it. A device that is off shows its plate dimmed, and its controls still turn.
When its owner cannot be reached The clip keeps its last content, dimmed, and cannot be edited. The device keeps its last picture, dimmed, and its light is dark.
When something fails The edit that failed stays in the editor. One line in the status bar says what failed. The value that failed returns to the owner's value. One line in the status bar says what failed.
What is kept The clip's content and settings are kept by its owner. The tab in front is kept with the set. The chain and its settings are kept by their owners. Which device stands expanded is kept with the set.

#16.6 Tracks, Session view and Arrangement view

Every mode draws its tracks the same way. Session view and Arrangement view are two views of the mode's one set (§10.2).

Mode Track Clip Stop (a row) Takes
Central A world. The set is the Day; its die is on the Main track. A page: a being, a thing or a flow. Pages you open together. Revisions: draft, saved, edited since save.
Factory An agent session. A task. A batch of tasks that launch together. Attempts. You choose the attempt that lands.
Expressions An Expression. A scene. A moment across several Expressions. Captured takes of a scene.
Technē A reading, a journey or the occurrences of a subject. An event, an occurrence or a revision at its time and place. A stop of a walk: it stands its event and launches the scenes it carries. Readings that extend a reading.
Live A part. A note clip or an audio clip. A row of clips. Take lanes.

The word scene always means an Expression's scene. A row of clips is a stop.

#The track

A track's head shows its colour, its name and, in Factory, its agent. Groups fold under one header; the members of a group step in below it, with one coloured rail for each level, and a row in a group launches all its children at once.

Under the head is the track's mixer row, after Live's. In Session view it stands under the slots. In Arrangement view the same controls stand at the right of the track's head, and the whole mixer can stand under the tracks, as in Live 12. The row runs in Live's sections, from the top:

Section Control Live's meaning
In/Out Input Where the track's material comes from.
In/Out Monitor In, Auto or Off: when you watch the track's input, and so what of the track streams to the monitors and the widgets.
In/Out Output Where the track's material goes: to the Main track by default, to a group, or nowhere. In Central, whether a world sends its work to the Day.
In/Out Works in Live has none; it routes as an output sent to a return track does. The workcell the track's agents work in: the gateway they reach their harness through, the machine that carries them, the seat they change and how their work lands (§19.23). A track takes its world's workcell until you choose another. The track's terminals and agent sessions live in that workcell's session spaces, and a Terminal opens in its room (§10.1).
Sends A knob for each return track How much of the track reaches a return track, whose chain several tracks share.
Volume and pan Volume, Pan The level and the place of the track's sound.
Switches Activator The track plays, or it does not. Off, it is silent and dimmed, and keeps its place and its settings.
Switches Solo You attend to the soloed tracks alone: only they show and sound. The others keep running.
Switches Arm The track records, and its agent writes directly, with receipts.

⌥⌘M shows or hides the mixer in either view, and ⌥⌘I, ⌥⌘S and ⌥⌘R show or hide the In/Out section, the sends and the return tracks. A mode draws only the sections its tracks have. Sends and return tracks are Live's. Volume and pan stand where there is sound, in Expressions and Live. Works in stands on every track an agent works on, in every mode. What each control means in each mode is in the mode's own section (§17.1–§21.1).

In Factory the workcells stand where Live keeps its return tracks, after the sessions and before the Main track, and ⌥⌘R shows or hides them. Each carries its own chain, which every session that works in it shares, and everything that belongs to the workcell stands on that chain: the machine, the seats and their checkouts, and what a run leaves behind. A session space is the workcell's, not the window's: it outlives the window, and a provider's name for it is a label (§10.1). In every mode, ▸ beside a track's Works in shows its workcell's chain in Device view.

The Main track sits at the end, where Live keeps it. It carries each row's launch button, Stop All, and Back to Arrangement, which lights when what plays differs from the ruler. Its own chain holds what works on the whole: the Day and Approvals in Central; the Run map, Approvals and the prompt pads in Factory.

#Session view

Session view is the grid: tracks across, rows down, everything launchable, nothing in a fixed order.

A clip that is Looks
Waiting A fast blink. It has no length, because nobody knows how long it will take.
Running A slow blink and a fill that grows. It has no end drawn.
Stopped Ready, in full colour.
Recording Marked with the record light.
Stalled Striped and frozen where its output stopped. The track lights a retry.
Done Dimmed and settled.

An empty slot is a place to write: double-click it to start a clip there. Each track has a stop button in its empty slots. In Factory, a track whose clip has stalled lights a retry, which starts again from the last good step on the same basis. How a clip launches, when it lands and what follows it are the clip's own, in its Launch tab. The transport's Quantize is the launch quantize for every clip set to Global. The number keys launch rows.

#Arrangement view

Arrangement view lays the same tracks along one ruler.

Mode The ruler measures
Central Today, from first entry to last.
Factory The time of the run. Each session has a needle at its last check-in.
Expressions The scenes in order, in seconds, with each Expression's picture lane over its sound lane, and audio tracks beside them on the same timeline, as a video editor holds picture and sound.
Technē The time of your sessions, or the history of what you study, from deep time to today, with readings as layers of tracks. It is Technē's timeline.
Live Bars and beats.

Under each track lie its lanes. U folds the selected track to one line, or opens it with its lanes again:

  • Automation lanes, one for each parameter that moves: an agent's effort over a run, a field device over a scene, the sky's pull on a filter. Each lane's head names its device and its parameter. Press A for Automation Mode: the track's head gains a device chooser and a parameter chooser, the chosen parameter's moves lie over the clips, and you draw them there. + on the head opens the chosen parameter in a lane of its own; − on a lane hides the lane and keeps its moves. Arm the track and move the parameter, and the move is recorded. A modulated parameter shows what moves it. A value you override gives control back only when you press Re-enable.
  • Take lanes, one for each take, as Live's are. Audition a take from its lane. Select a stretch of a take and press Return to copy it into the main lane: that is how you choose the attempt that lands, the capture that stands, or the revision you keep. The main lane shows which take each stretch came from. ⌥⌘U shows or hides the take lanes.
  • Event lanes, in Factory: each session's messages, files, terminal and pages read. Click an event and it opens beside the ruler.

A needle jumps each time its agent checks in, and a needle that does not move marks a stall: the thread freezes where its output stopped. A line marks now, and Follow keeps it in view.

Named sections run along the top; in Technē they are epochs, they nest, and the narrowest colours the clips inside it. A marker is a named, coloured point. A loop region has an in point and an out point: the transport plays, and repeats, only between them. Punch in and punch out mark where recording may happen, as in Live; in Factory they mark the window in which agents may write.

A clip stays the same thing wherever you move it. A move changes only where it stands in time.

Edit What it does
Move, insert Moves the clip and shifts the clips after it.
Move, overwrite Moves the clip and replaces what was there.
Trim Drags an edge to change the length.
Roll Moves the seam between two clips. One grows by what the other loses.
Slip Changes where the clip starts inside its own content.
Slide Moves a clip between fixed neighbours.
Split Cuts the clip in two at the playhead. The lengths add up to the original.

A void is a still clip, not a gap. Every edit is one labelled step in the undo list; a split or a roll is one step, not three. Snap pulls the playhead and the edges you drag to clip edges, markers, loop edges and the playhead; hold Alt to turn it off while you drag.

Setting Values Default What it does
Tracks shown Any set of the mode's tracks All The tracks in view.
Lanes Takes, Automation, Events, each On · Off Takes On, Automation On, Events Off The lanes under the tracks.
Time scale Even · Stretched Even Stretched keeps deep time readable beside today.
Zoom Any span Fit all The span in view.
Snap On · Off On Aligns dragged items to edges, markers and the playhead.
Move mode Insert · Overwrite Insert What a move does to its neighbours.
Trim mode Trim · Roll · Slip · Slide Trim What an edge drag does.
Overview strip On · Off On The whole ruler, with the view marked.
Standing floor Facts only · Plus claims · Plus inferences · Plus guesses · All All In Technē, hides clips that stand below the level.

#Rules

  • A track holds the material of its owner. The views show it and never copy it.
  • Switching between Session view, Arrangement view and Pane view changes neither the selection nor what runs.
  • A pane you leave keeps its place. Come back to it, by view or by mode, and it stands with the camera, the selection and the moment it had.
  • A clip that is running shows no end. A waiting clip shows no length. A stalled clip shows where it stopped and does not look done.
  • A row launches only what is in it. Stop pressed twice cancels at once; launch quantize does not delay it.
  • Solo changes what you attend to, never what runs. The activator decides whether a track plays; its Output decides where its work goes.
  • A move does not change what a clip is. Placement does not raise a claim to a fact.
  • Every edit is one labelled step that can be undone alone.
  • The overview strip is the one way to move along the whole ruler. No second scrub bar stands beside it.
  • Every mode uses the same states, the same stop buttons and the same keys.

#16.7 The browser and the pool

There is one browser, the same in every mode (§10.3). It holds four kinds of thing: material, instruments with their presets, devices, and running things. Material comes from the mode's owners and leads the list; the other kinds follow in the same order in every mode, each grouped by the product that makes it. Its Places, You, Agents, Machines and Work, are where your ground lies. A mode's section adds no browser of its own.

Act How What happens
Preview Select a row once. Its preview shows at the foot of the list. Nothing changes.
Open Double-click it, or drag it into a pane. Material opens in its instrument; an instrument opens full in the pane.
Bring into the set Drag material onto an empty track. It joins the set: a world joins today, a chat's session reopens where it stopped.
Make this mode's clip Drag a constellation onto a track. The mode makes its own clip of it, with the constellation as its source: a page, a task, a scene, an event or a Live clip.
Show in Browser Choose it beside a clip's Constellation, or in the clip's menu. The browser selects the clip's constellation, and keeps it selected when you change mode.
Start from a template Open a template from the browser. A new set starts with the template's tracks and its layout.
Start a track Drag an instrument, or one of its presets, onto an empty track. A track starts with it, as in Live. An agent dropped there takes the seat.
Add Drag a device onto a chain, or a monitor onto the rail. It stands where you dropped it.
Keep at hand Drag a running thing or a chat onto the rail. Its tile opens on the rail.
Bring in a project Add folder… in the Work place. Setup's Projects step opens for that folder (§10.11).

#The pool

The pool stands under the browser in every mode, where Live keeps its Groove Pool, and holds the DLW's grooves: QL frames and MEF lenses. A frame is the form of a whole and the roles round it (§17.4). A lens is one of Quaternal Logic's twelve ways of seeing, with its six sublenses (§17.11). Each reads a clip without changing it, as a groove shapes how a clip plays without changing its notes.

Column Values What it does
Name A frame or a lens, on its colour The groove. One that the selected clip uses is lit.
Hot-swap A button Tries another frame or lens on the selected clip while it plays.
Sublenses A lens's six sublenses A lens's parameters. Turn them to read the clip more finely.
Commit A button Writes the selected clip's reading into the wiki, through its owner, where the constellation keeps it for every mode.

To take a frame or a lens out of a constellation, drag the constellation from the browser, or from a clip's Constellation, onto the pool: its frame and its lenses stand there, as a clip dropped on Live's pool gives up its groove. To read a clip through one, choose it in the clip's Groove (§16.5). Applying it never changes the clip's source, and nothing is written into the wiki until you press Commit.

In Live mode the set's own grooves stand beside the frames and lenses, as Live's do: Groove, Base, Quantize, Timing, Random and Velocity for each, Global Amount at the foot, and "Drop clips or grooves here" when there are none. Each groove is the set's, read from it and written into it, and its Commit writes the groove into the clip's notes.

  • The pool holds QL frames and MEF lenses and, in Live, the set's grooves. It holds no device, no instrument and no pane's contents.
  • A frame or a lens reads a clip. It never changes the clip's source.
  • Only Commit writes, and it writes the reading into the wiki through its owner.
  • How the window stands is kept with the set. An arrangement to start from again is a template in the browser (§10.3).
  • A set keeps where things stand and what each pane holds, by reference to their owners, never their content. Opened again, it asks each owner afresh, so nothing shows from the set alone; what it could not keep, such as a draft never saved, it names as it opens.

#16.8 Play, record and automation

Play launches clips. Each clip's track runs through its chain, and the instrument makes its part: the agent runs, the field plays, the walk walks. Record lays what played into Arrangement view as clips, with takes under them.

Arm, then move any parameter of any device, and the move is recorded as an automation lane on that track. You can automate an agent's effort over a run, the pace of a walk, a field device over a scene, the sky's pull on a filter. Arrangement view shows each track's clips, and under them the lanes of its devices. A clip can carry envelopes of its own, which move a parameter over the clip's own time. Re-enable gives a parameter back to its lane, or to the agent or instrument that held it. A modulated parameter shows what moves it.

A pad triggers: press it and it plays now, as a Drum Rack pad does. When something happens later is a matter of time, and time has three homes: a clip's place on the ruler, an automation lane, and a routine in Settings, Automations (§10.10). No pad and no device keeps a clock time of its own.

Five times run through the DLW, and they are kept apart. The day is Central's: when it opens and when it closes. The sky and the clock are Quaternal Logic's: where the planets stand and where the wheel has turned. A routine runs at the time Settings gives it, and each run lies on the ruler as a clip beside the rest of the work; only what was set to run fires, and only what fired is drawn. The transport moves over clips and drives nothing else. An occasion is a moment you stand in: it keeps that moment as it was read, and says separately whether what it shows still stands now. Any device may read any of these times, and a modulator may take one as its source. One time becomes another only by a rule stated for that crossing: the transport never moves the day, and a past occasion never passes for now.

#16.9 How a device looks

A designed face, not a form. A device's parameters are its contract with its owner. Its panel is drawn by hand for that device, as every Live device is. A list of parameters drawn one under the other is the fallback, and only for a device that ships no panel of its own. Live does the same for a plug-in that has no editor.

The picture comes first. Most panels have a display: a dark well that draws the device's state from its live values. EQ Eight draws its curve, Auto Filter its filter, Wavetable its wave. Handles in the well are controls: drag the picture and the parameter moves. The other controls stand round the display, in sections.

One height, many widths. On a chain, every device has the same height. The width comes from what the device holds. A small effect is narrow, and an instrument with two displays is wide.

Nothing scrolls, and no box sits inside a box. Sections are columns, ruled off from each other by a hairline and named in small capitals. The well is the only inset surface. When a panel holds more than fits, it gets pages in its head, as Wavetable has Osc 1 and Osc 2. The shown page's face slides to the page you chose.

Values are short. A control shows a number, a unit or a word. A sentence never appears in a panel. What a control does is said in the status bar when you point at it.

The panel answers three questions. Its arrangement shows what the device changes, how its controls relate, and what result you are watching. Related parameters sit together. A mode that changes what a parameter means changes the panel visibly. A label is a word for the thing, never a tidied-up key.

#Measures

All measures are in pixels at 100 %. The grid is 4 px.

Part Measure
Head 22 high
Band (the body on a chain) 168 high
Plate on a chain 191 high: head, band and borders
Control column 56 wide
Dial 28 square, a 270° ring
Value box 16 high, 50 wide or more
Toggle, radio button, chooser, action 16 high
Hit area of any control 22 or more in each direction
Row of a list 17 high
Display on a compact plate 140 × 146
Whole expanded The detail area's width. One band high, its bands side by side; a display may grow the band up to half the height of the panes.
Pop-out window 1180 × 640 when it first opens, then the size you leave it at. Whole is docked under the material, one band high.
Section label 9 px capitals, 13 high
Names and values 10 to 11 px
Folded strip 22 wide
Widget tile 136 × 136, or 280 × 136

The plate does not reflow. When the detail area is shorter or taller, the whole plate scales between 80 % and 125 %, as Live's zoom scales its devices.

#The head

From left to right:

  1. Activator. A round light. Amber: the owner reports the device on. Grey: the owner reports it off. A hollow ring: the owner has not said. Press it to ask the owner to turn the device on or off. The light changes only when the owner answers.
  2. Expanded view ▸, Live's toggle. Double-click the head to fold the device to its title.
  3. Name. A rack shows its set's name: "Skills · build-lane".
  4. Held mark. The name of whoever holds values on this device, in the stall colour.
  5. Pages. One tab for each page. The shown page joins the body's face. A page can carry its own light, as Hybrid Reverb's EQ tab does.
  6. The device's own acts, such as the Studio's Save and Undo.
  7. Rail, ▦ Pane, ↗ Pop out, at the right (§16.4).

Right-click the head for Save as preset, Hot-swap, Show automation and Map.

#The body

The body is one band on a chain. Whole, expanded or in a window, sets its bands side by side. A band is a row of sections. A section is a column of controls with a label. The display stands in a section of its own, at the left.

#Colours

Colour Means
Face The body of the plate.
Head Lighter than the face. Tinted blue when the device is selected.
Field The ground of value boxes, toggles and choosers.
Well The display. Near black.
Teal A value: a dial's arc, a value box's fill, a curve, a reach for reading.
Amber On: a toggle, a chosen radio button, the activator, a handle, a reach for writing.
Green An owner's yes: a skill admitted, a task done.
Orange Someone else holds this value.
Red Automation, and the record button.

A device does not bring colours of its own. A colour inside a display carries a meaning of the material, as a track's colour does.

#16.10 Controls and the hand

A panel uses these controls and no others.

Control Use it for It shows Live's nearest
Dial A number that you sweep The name above, a 270° ring with a teal arc, the value below. A value that can turn either way starts its arc at zero. A knob.
Value box A number where space is short, or one you set exactly The value in a field that fills teal to its place in the range. A slider, such as Wavetable's Volume.
Toggle On or off The name in a box, amber when on. Auto Filter's Hz button.
Radio One of two to five Buttons side by side or stacked; the chosen one amber, and the amber slides to a new choice. A choice the owner cannot take stands dimmed, and the status bar says why. Auto Filter's filter types.
Chooser One of many The value and ▾; a menu. A closed choice is dimmed in the menu, with its reason. Wavetable's wavetable menu.
Swatch A colour The colour in a small square, then its value. Press it to pick another. A clip's or a track's colour.
Rows A list: a rack's chains, a scope's places One row each: your request as a square; the owner's answer as a light, or the member's kind mark in its state; the name; a short meter; a short note. A long list pages. Where the order is yours, the chosen row carries a grip and ▲ ▼; drag the grip, or press ⌥↑ ⌥↓, to move it. A rack's chain list.
Ladder Evidence in steps One tick for each step: lit where it is established, dark where it is not, hollow where nobody has observed it. A level meter's segments.
Readout A reading A short value over its name. A large readout is the count that the view is for. A readout you may copy shows a copy mark when you point at it. Hybrid Reverb's "100 % / 285 ms".
Action Something done once The name in an outlined box. An act that you cannot undo is held, not clicked. A momentary button.
Light A state that the owner reports A small round light. A light that is working carries a ring. A chain's activator.
Handle A parameter that you move on the picture An amber ring, numbered in order of importance. EQ Eight's band dots.
Pad Two numbers that belong together A square well with one handle. The name and the value of each side stand along its edges: across is one number, up is the other. A faint line at each side's default. A synth's X/Y pad.

The same moves work on every control that holds a number.

Do Result
Drag up or down The value moves. The whole range is 160 px. A stepped value moves one step for each 14 px.
Hold Shift while you drag The value moves ten times more slowly.
Double-click The value returns to its default.
Focus it and press ↑ ↓ or ← → One step, or 1 % of the range.
Focus it and type a number The value is set exactly. Enter sends it; Esc keeps the value you had.
Page Up, Page Down 10 % of the range.
Home, End The minimum, the maximum.
Delete The default.
Point at it The status bar says its name and what it does.

A dial suits one number. Where an operation is a relation or a place, the panel shows the relation or the place itself and lets you move it there.

A handle moves in the directions that its picture shows. A handle for two parameters, such as gravity across and up, moves in two directions. The arrow keys move a focused handle 2 px, or 0.5 px with Shift.

Where a picture shows two numbers at one point, one handle moves both. The filter's handle sits at its cutoff across and its resonance up. The dynamics curve's knee sits at its threshold across and its makeup up, and the dip in its time display is as deep as its ratio. The delay's first repeat stands at its time across and its mix up; the second, at twice the time across and its feedback up. Where the picture does not show both, a pad does: the reverb's Room pad has the decay across and the size up. Press the handle and drag, or press anywhere in the pad and the handle comes there. Hold Shift for a tenth of the speed. The arrow keys move the handle 1 % of a side, and Page Up and Page Down 10 % of the vertical. Home and End go to the left and right edges. Delete or a double-click returns both numbers to their defaults.

#A change and its answer

While you drag, the control shows the value you set. When you release it, the new value goes to the owner; a key press sends at once. Until the owner confirms the value, it shows in italics. If the owner refuses, the control returns to the owner's value, and the status bar gives the owner's reason.

Some changes ask you first. When you raise a scope's reach, the new reach waits, drawn dashed, with Confirm and Cancel beside it. Nothing is sent until you confirm, and Confirm is held, not clicked (below).

#How a control moves

A control moves only when its state changes, and only to show that change. Nothing moves by itself. Nothing makes you wait.

Your hand is always answered at once. A drag, a key, a double-click: the value is there as you set it, and nothing eases it. What something else changed, the owner, an agent, the sky, a modulator, glides or rings once, so that you see it changed. The times are the same everywhere.

What changes How it moves
A value you set At once. It never eases under your hand.
A value that something else sets The arc, the fill or a pad's handle glides to it in 0.12 s, and a thin ring stands round the control for a second. Where the host says who moved it, the name stands on the control for two seconds.
A choice: a radio, a head's pages The amber, or the page's face, slides to the new choice in 0.2 s.
A light It fills or empties in 0.16 s.
A light that is working A ring spreads from it and fades, again and again, for as long as the owner reports the device, or the row, working. When the owner stops, the ring stops.
A reading that has not come yet The empty ring or field breathes, slowly. A reading you already had shows at once and is asked for again behind it. The control never says Loading.
A step of a ladder that is being worked on Its tick pulses.
Rows that come, go, move or change Each row slides to its place in 0.18 s, and a new row fades up. A short meter grows or shrinks to its new value.
A device opens or folds ▸ turns to ▾ in 0.2 s.
A copy The mark turns to a tick for a moment, then back.

A default is a detent. A value box shows its default as a tick, and a dial as a notch on its ring. A drag that passes close to the default lands on it and the tick brightens; go on dragging and the hand leaves it. Hold Shift to drag past it. A stepped value has no detent: each step is its own stop. A pad keeps the detent on each side: its default is a faint line, and the handle catches on the line as it crosses.

An act that you cannot undo is held. Raising a scope's reach, answering an approval, and taking a device off its chain wait for you, and each is a hold. Press the name and keep it down, or hold Space or Enter. A fill sweeps across the name in 0.9 s, and the act happens when it reaches the end. Let go early and it springs back, and nothing happens. An act that you can undo is never held.

Waiting keeps its width. A control that has sent its change and waits for the owner shows a ring turning over its name. Nothing around it moves.

Rows that you order carry a grip beside ▲ ▼ on the chosen row. Drag the grip and the other rows make room for it; ⌥↑ ⌥↓ still move the row one place.

A request for reduced motion stops all of it. Nothing glides, slides, rings or spins. What it showed stays: a working light keeps a still ring, a rung being worked on stays half lit, a reading that has not come stays dimmed, a name still stands for two seconds and goes, and the hold still fills, so that you can see how long to hold.

#16.11 Standing

Besides its value, a control shows who moves it.

Standing How it shows What you do
Automated A red dot at the control's top left. Move it to override the lane.
Overridden A hollow red dot. The transport's Re-enable lights. Press Re-enable to give the value back to its lane.
Modulated A thin outer arc on the dial: the range that the modulator moves the value through. The status bar names the modulator. A modulator never overwrites the value you set: the dial keeps it, and the arc shows where the modulator has taken it. Set the centre of the range with the dial.
Held The arc or the fill in orange, and the holder's name under the control. Press the name to give the value back.
Moved A ring round the control for a second, and the name of what moved it for two seconds. Nothing. Move it back if you want it back.
Waiting The value in italics, the arc dashed. Wait for the owner, or move it again.
Disabled The control at 40 % strength. The status bar says why. Do what the reason says.
Working A ring spreading from the light, for as long as the owner reports it. Nothing. Wait, or stop it with the device's own act.
Waiting for a reading The empty ring or field breathes. Nothing. The owner is being asked.
No reading A hollow light. Nothing. The owner has not said.

#16.12 The display

  • Draw every mark from the device's values or readings, by the device's own law. Do not draw a likely picture.
  • When a reading is missing, say which one in the well. Do not draw it as zero.
  • Give a compact display at least one handle: the one parameter that you most often move. Give a whole display a handle for each parameter that the picture can show.
  • Number the handles 1, 2 and on, in order of importance.
  • Put axis labels inside the well, small and faint. Put one short reading at the top right.
  • Say a number once in a view. The corner gives way to any number that a dial, a box, a readout or a pad in the same plate already shows: it is the reading for a display that has nothing beside it, as in the widget and the pane. A readout does not repeat what the picture writes beside its own mark.
  • Give a pair of numbers that belong together one pad, or one handle where the picture shows both, rather than two dials side by side.
  • Expanded and in a window, let the display take the room and keep the controls at their size, as an expanded EQ Eight does.
  • Move the picture only when its readings move. Respect a request for reduced motion.
  • A rack's picture is its chain list.

#16.13 What a device brings

A device brings these to the shell:

  1. Its parameters, each declared under the device's own id: key, name, kind, range or values, default, unit, group, whether it is a macro, and its write path. A parameter without a write path is a reading.
  2. Its kind and its views, built from the panel kit: the views of the places it stands in (§16.3). A device on a chain brings folded, compact and whole; one with material of its own brings full, and a pop-out where it needs its own; one kept at hand brings its widget. A monitor brings its widget and its full, and nothing else.
  3. Its displays and their handles.

The shell brings the values, the writes, the navigation between views, the room each view stands in, and the standing of each parameter: its automation, its modulator, its holder.

The shell knows no product by name. Each product brings its devices, its rows in the browser, its material for the tracks and its tiles through the same door as a device you build yourself, so a new product joins without any change to the shell. No product gets a place of its own outside these.

The panel kit is packages/live-shell/ui/src/inhabitants/sdk/panel.tsx, and a designed device is a module of inhabitants/catalogue/panels/. A device without views of its own is drawn by the generic plate: its parameters, grouped, in the order the device declares them.

#A parameter earns its place

A parameter stays on a device only when all of these are true:

  • An owner operation stands behind it: a write that the owner exposes, or a reading that the owner reports. A word for a quality, such as thoroughness or boldness, is not a parameter unless such an operation stands behind it.
  • Its control fits its values. Use a dial or a value box for a quantity that varies smoothly. Use a stepped dial, a radio or a chooser for a few states, and a toggle for two. Do not draw a range or a step that the owner does not have.
  • When you move it, something that you can see or hear changes: the display, the material or a reading.
  • Its default is the owner's default. Reset returns to that default, never to a guessed zero.
  • A value the owner reports outside the control's useful range shows as it is. The control never clamps or rewrites it.
  • A macro moves real parameters, each within its own range.
  • It does not repeat another device's parameter. Where two devices would hold the same setting, one holds it and the other shows it as a reading.

A device whose owner has no smooth quantity has no dials. Its compact controls are its real discrete ones. A rack of skills has no risk knob: it has your requests, a scope, and a preview that you apply.

#Kind marks

A device that holds things of several kinds shows each thing's kind, not a picture of its name. Carried practice has four kinds, each with its woodcut mark: a skill, a method, a methodology and a skillset (§19.7). The person chooses one of the two sets of marks, the blade or the pen, and the whole shell uses it. A mark has three states, and its drawing does not change: a full line for available, the line in orange for held back for a reason that you can clear, a dim line for withheld.

#16.14 When a device is done

A device is done when all of these are true:

  • Its views draw in the device gallery on its declared parameters, and move together. It draws no view of a place it does not stand in.
  • On a chain, Whole reads expanded above the chain, and the pop-out window shows the material with every control. A monitor's Full carries every one of its settings in its head.
  • Every control says what it does in the status bar, and works from the keyboard.
  • Nothing scrolls inside a plate, and no box sits inside a box.
  • The compact view has four macros or fewer.
  • The display draws from values, and its handles move the parameters they show.
  • The views match the device's entry below, and the entry passes the fence (§16.17).
  • Beside its Live nearest, the plate reads as a Live device.
  • The whole it belongs to works as a person uses it, walked from start to end by someone other than its builder. A part that passes on its own does not pass the whole, and every step of the walk it belongs to still has to hold.

To see a device in the gallery, run the gallery from packages/live-shell/ui:

npx vite --config src/inhabitants/catalogue/vite.config.mjs

Then open ?device=<family>:<face>&view=all, or name the views you want: &view=flip,popout. Add &generic=1 to see the generic plate of the same device.

#16.15 Six reference devices

Six devices show the whole pattern. Each runs on a labelled fixture. Move a control in one view and the others follow. Point at a control to read what it does, in the line under the views.

Device Kind It shows Live's nearest
Day Instrument A display that you click. Pages that are two things at once: today's Day and tomorrow's. Macros of four kinds. Hybrid Reverb
Torus Instrument A picture drawn by the law that it plays. Handles on the picture. An envelope display. A modulation arc and an automation dot. Wavetable
Physics Effect A law drawn as a diagram with a two-way handle. Pages for a long set of parameters. Macros on the widget. Auto Filter, Corpus
Skillset rack Rack The chain list as the picture. Each member's kind mark and evidence. Your request beside the owner's answer. Preview, then apply. Audio Effect Rack
